US_NSCW_19th_2021_Ghost_GA_FL.overview: First- and second-generation immigrants from England, Germany, and Ireland endured violence, disease, and social conflicts to build a new life in Georgia and northern Florida. After setting up a society that relied heavily on enslaved Black labor and cotton production, they saw its bloody collapse during the Civil War. The jobs and money that came with World War II brought new economic life to the region, and decades of sharecropping, recovery, and segregation finally began to give way to cities, suburban life, and civil rights for Black residents.

NE-NJ-NY_NY2024_CentralUpstate_Ghost.overview: Years of war, crop failures, and religious or economic persecution pushed many Europeans to migrate to North America. Settlers cleared land, built farms and towns, and sometimes exchanged knowledge with Indigenous nations. After the American Revolution, families moved west into the Midwest, while treaties and wars forced Indigenous peoples from their homelands. Growing cities became centers of trade and industry, linked by canals and railroads. New waves of immigrants and African Americans continued to reshape work, culture, and daily life in a rapidly changing nation.

AFAM182021_1.1.3_1.1.4_Ghost.name: Early Louisiana Creoles & African Americans

subjourneys.AFAM182021_1.1.3: Central & Southern Louisiana Creoles & African Americans

AFAM182021_1.1.3_1.1.4_Ghost.overview: Early South Louisiana was home to a large population of West Africans and Creoles, a distinct ethnic group of people with mixed European, Indigenous, and West African ancestry. During the French and Spanish colonial eras, thousands of enslaved Black and Indigenous people labored on sugar and indigo plantations in rural areas and did other work in urban New Orleans. After the Civil War, many Afro-Creoles and Black freedmen left the South in hopes of finding freedom and work. Today, Louisiana Creoles have a unique culture with their own French-based language and world-renowned music and culinary traditions.

MENA2023_4.2.name: Egypt
MENA2023_4.2.overview: Many know of Pharaonic Egypt’s Pyramids of Giza and the palaces of Luxor, but fewer are aware that Muslims, Christians, and Jews all contributed to the history of this ancient land. The earliest records of Jewish civilization come from Egypt in the 13th century BCE. Egypt was also an early home to Christianity, which was preached in the land by Mark the Evangelist. Known as “Copts” from the Arabic word for Egyptians, these Christians have preserved their church and religious rituals from the first century onwards. With the Muslim conquest of Egypt of the seventh century CE, Islam and Arabic have also shaped the history and culture of Egypt. Egypt is one of the oldest and most respected centers of the Muslim global community.

US_NSCW_19th_2021_1.7.4.name: Southern Utah & Arizona Settlers

subjourneys.US_NSCW_19th_2021_1.7.4.1: Southern Arizona & Northwestern Chihuahua Mexico Settlers

US_NSCW_19th_2021_1.7.4.overview: Escaping religious persecution, members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (or Mormons) entered Utah territory in 1847, colonizing and building settlements in many surrounding areas. Latter-day Saints were often immigrants from western European countries in the United Kingdom and western Europe. Over the next several decades, converts to the religion immigrated to Utah and spread south to areas in Arizona, California, Nevada, Idaho, Montana, southern Alberta (Canada), and northern Mexico. In doing so, they transformed deserts, valleys, and mountains and populated them with cities and towns.

ASIA2023_1.3.3.2.name: Mascarene Islands
ASIA2023_1.3.3.2.overview: Located in the southwestern Indian Ocean, the Mascarene Islands—including Mauritius, Réunion, and Rodrigues—have been shaped by their volcanic origins, maritime connections, and diverse cultures. Historically, these islands witnessed colonization, slavery, indentured servitude, and waves of migration—eventually evolving into the diverse societies they are today. While sugar plantations dominated their economies during the colonial era, independence from European powers brought new challenges and opportunities. Today, the Mascarenes are known for their rugged natural landscapes and cultural diversity, which can be seen in the islands’ cuisine, religious practices, and annual celebrations.

US_NSCW_19th_2021_1.7.2.overview: Settlers of Northern Utah and Southeast Idaho were largely converts to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints from New England and Great Britain. The culture of those two regions, and later of Scandinavia, informed the social worlds of Northern Utah and Southeast Idaho. Settlement began in the early 1850s and spread northward into Alberta, Canada. Mass migrations to these sites ended by the 1920s.

MENA2023_2.2.1.name: Morocco & Western Algeria
MENA2023_2.2.1.overview: The Maghrib, historically known as the westernmost region of the Islamic world, is a diverse area with a rich cultural history. Arabic is the official language of most North African countries, but Amazigh languages and culture remain an integral part of the region’s identity. In Morocco, up to 60 percent of the population has Amazigh heritage, while in Algeria, the figure is around 30 percent. The Maghrib is also home to a variety of other ethnicities from Europe and Sub-Saharan Africa. Located in the western Mediterranean region, it maintains historical and contemporary ties to Europe and Sub-Saharan Africa. Since ancient times, the region has been a center of trade, cultural exchange, and migration.

LA2023_Chile_Ghost.name: Chile
LA2023_Chile_Ghost.overview: Chile is a country of extremes—a long and narrow strip of land perched between the Andes Mountains and the Pacific Ocean. Its identity has been shaped by the long and often violent interactions between Spanish colonists and the resilient Mapuche people, then later transformed by migration. Throughout their history, Chileans have adapted to survive everything from devastating earthquakes to profound political divisions. This national character is expressed in the pride of the rural huaso (cowboys), the ingenuity of its working people, and a rich artistic heritage that gives voice to both its struggles and its triumphs.

FRAM2019_4.1.overview: Over a century and a half of settlement, the Acadians established a prosperous and dynamic society in what became Canada’s Maritime Provinces, but it was shattered when England and France went to war. The Acadians were forcibly removed from their homeland by the British and scattered along the Atlantic Seaboard. Some returned to find their old farmland taken over by Anglo settlers, while others established Acadian enclaves in New England. In both places, they worked to preserve their language and culture even in the face of persecution.

SouthAfrica_top.2.name: South Africa, European Settlers
SouthAfrica_top.2.overview: The English took over the Dutch colony of Cape Town in the early 19th century and spent the next 160 years trying to establish dominance in the region. English soldiers, farmers, government officials, and unmarried women moved to the colony seeking new opportunities and to strengthen the British Empire. The 8,000 mile separation from England often fostered a fierce devotion to the British crown in English South Africans, and the importance of what it meant to be English took on increased significance.

MENA2019_1.6.4.name: Eastern Africa
MENA2019_1.6.4.overview: Eastern Africa was home to African farmers, herders, and craftspeople in the interior and Arab and South Asian traders in cities along the coast. As European nations carved the continent into protectorates and colonies, they changed both the landscape and society, disrupting or destroying traditional modes of life and work. After throwing off colonial rule in the 1960s, East Africans continue to reshape their lives and land to lay claim to both their traditional pasts and modern opportunities.

MENA2023_2.2.4.name: Algeria
MENA2023_2.2.4.overview: Today’s Algeria, the largest country on the African continent, has a diverse geography, climate, and people. It maintains important historical and contemporary ties to Europe, North Africa, and Sub-Saharan Africa. Since ancient times, the densely populated cities of the northern coast of Algeria made it a center for trade and the movement of people between Africa and its European neighbors. Its name derives from its capital city, Algiers, which in Arabic means “the islands”—a reference to the four islands off the coast of this ancient port city.

MENA2023_2.2.5.name: Tunisia & Western Libya
MENA2023_2.2.5.overview: Tunisia and Libya occupy the southern shores of the central Mediterranean, lands that, since ancient times, have been home to many different peoples. From the Phoenician settlement of North Africa in 1000 BC to the more recent Arab conquest and settlement of this region in the 8th century, today’s Tunisia and Libya boast a rich history. While both countries have been shaped by millennia of migration and the rise and fall of empires, the majority of the population today identifies as Arab, though with diverse cultural expressions and traditions. Significant Amazigh communities also maintain distinct cultural identities, languages, and traditions, particularly in Libya, and have played an important role in the region.

AFAM192021_1.4.10.name: Afro-Bermudians
AFAM192021_1.4.10.overview: When the British first began settling Bermuda in 1609, it had never been inhabited previously. The islands’ first Black inhabitants were from the Spanish West Indies. They were joined by enslaved people captured by privateers and some who escaped from slave vessels. Most had ancestral roots in West Africa. Black Bermudians, both enslaved and free, have been the island’s majority population since the early 1800s. But only at the end of the 20th century did they begin to enjoy equal status with white Bermudians.

AFAM192021_1.7.overview: Many Black people were trafficked to the Gulf Coast from West Africa and the Caribbean by European enslavers. In the early 18th-century, they arrived at the ports of New Orleans, Biloxi, and Mobile as forced labor to build the struggling French colony of Louisiana. During the Spanish period, enslaved people could buy their freedom, and New Orleans became home to the largest free Black population in North America. After the Civil War, most African Americans and Afro-Creoles became sharecroppers or wage laborers. Some owned businesses. Others escaped Southern racial violence by moving north and west, where descendant communities remain today.

LA2023_BrazilSouth_Ghost.overview: Portuguese colonists began arriving in southern Brazil in the early 1500s, and since the 1700s, many of their descendants have lived on farms and celebrated a gaúcho, or cowboy, culture. Others lived in cities like Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, with strong ties to Portugal through Catholicism, colonial architecture, food, and commerce. As cities have grown, so has a sense of Brazilian identity that takes pride in its mixed racial and cultural milieu and the beauty of the landscape. Today, southern Brazil remains a hub of commerce, industry, and culture.

subjourneys.AFAM192021_1.4.2: Windward Islands to Costal Venezuela & Guyana

AFAM192021_1.4.2_1.4.4_1.4.5_1.4.10_Ghos.overview: The people of the Lesser Antilles are primarily of Afro-Caribbean descent. Many of their ancestors were ripped from their lives in West Africa, enslaved, and brought to the Americas to work on sugar and other plantations. Despite the violence and terror of slavery, Afro-Caribbean peoples maintained cultural traditions from Africa, sometimes blending them with the music and food of British and French colonizers. Ultimately, this created a culture that has spread throughout the small islands of the Caribbean as well as Panama and Guyana.

ASIA2023_1.3.15.name: Asians in South Africa
ASIA2023_1.3.15.overview: In and around the Cape of Good Hope, and later, across South Africa, waves of migration from Asia and elsewhere in Africa intersected with colonial Dutch and British settlement, creating a uniquely mixed culture from the 1700s onwards. In the initial years of European settlement, Dutch farmers, Khoekhoe herders, and enslaved people from Madagascar, India, and Indonesia established a mixed community on the Cape. Their interactions birthed new elements of South African culture. Waves of Indian migration also helped set the stage for a professional, middle-class community. And while apartheid later enforced segregation, these diverse Asian influences created a society shaped by its earlier cultural mixing.

US_NSCW_18th_2021_2.3.4.overview: Colonists who settled along the Chesapeake Bay generally worked on tobacco plantations. Those from England were often poor, funding their Atlantic crossing by working as indentured servants. Those from what is now Germany frequently came to escape war and religious oppression. Around the Revolutionary War, these settlers moved southwest through the Great Appalachian Valley, putting down roots in the mountains of western North Carolina and eastern Tennessee by forcing Indigenous peoples from their homelands and seizing the land. They worked subsistence farms for generations. In the early 1900s, many people lost their farms and took work in cities and mill towns. World War II improved job access and prompted some people to move to Northern industrial cities.

US_NSCW_19th_2021_1.1.4.overview: The Gulf Coast and Lower Mississippi Valley has a rich history. Originally, Native American groups like the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Creek dominated the area. The climate, water access, and fertile soil enticed Scots-Irish farmers from the Carolinas to grow cotton and sugar. Their entry pushed Indigenous Peoples farther west and drastically increased the number of enslaved Africans to work plantations. By the turn of the 20th century, new opportunities in oil, lumber, and shipbuilding helped develop towns and larger cities in this culturally and socially diverse region.

US_NSCW_19th_2021_Ghost_VA.overview: English, German, and Scots-Irish immigrants headed to Virginia in droves. As European populations grew and land became more scarce, many immigrants and their descendants pushed further west and south—often pushing Inidgenous peoples out and bringing enslaved workers with them. Hardy frontier folk became small farmers, coal miners, and factory workers. Two world wars and the Great Depression led them even further afield, to industrial cities and urban suburbs.

CA2023_3.overview: As early as the 16th century, abundant cod drew seasonal fishermen from southern England to Newfoundland, where Indigenous peoples, including the Beothuk and Mi'kmaq, had long lived. Some settled permanently, driven by economic hardships and overpopulation in England. Though farming proved challenging on the island, fishing could provide a livelihood. Throughout the 1800s, Newfoundlanders expanded into seal hunting, shipbuilding, and fur trapping. Eventually, overreliance on natural resources weakened the economy, spurring many to move away. Newfoundlanders sought work in Nova Scotia and American cities like Boston and New York. Following Confederation, communities of expatriate Newfoundlanders also grew in major Canadian cities like Toronto.

ASIA2023_1.6.3.name: South Asians in Jamaica
ASIA2023_1.6.3.overview: Starting in the 18th century, Jamaica was transformed by imperialism, mass migration, and decolonization. After its Indigenous Arawak population was replaced by enslaved Africans and a small number of white plantation owners from the British Isles, the island's population grew to fuel the global sugar industry. The abolition of slavery in 1838 led to the arrival of Indian and Chinese indentured workers. By the early 20th century, many Jamaicans were moving to urban centers and migrating overseas, but Jamaican culture had worldwide influence after its independence in 1962.

Mexico_2021_1.1.6.name: Yucatán
Mexico_2021_1.1.6.overview: The Yucatán Peninsula is home to some of the oldest civilizations in the Americas, civilizations dating back thousands of years. The arrival of the Spanish conquistadors and the enslaved West Africans they brought with them changed the social and cultural landscape. The Indigenous Maya, who constituted the majority of the region’s population in pre-colonial times, became the primary labor force, harvesting sugar cane, logwood, and henequén. Over the years, wars and  economic crises drove many to leave rural Yucatán for urban centers like Mexico City and New York, where they found a growing middle class, jobs, and access to higher education.

ASIA2023_1.6.2.name: Lesser Antilles & Guyana
ASIA2023_1.6.2.overview: In the Lesser Antilles and Guyana, diverse Caribbean societies emerged from colonial plantation economies. In the 1750s, islands like Martinique, Guadeloupe, Barbados, and Antigua were sharply split between European colonists and enslaved Africans. After slavery's end, white plantation owners recruited Indian workers to places like British Guiana and Trinidad, bringing Hindu and Muslim influences to the islands. While sugar dominated the region’s economies, each island developed differently. By the 1950s, as independence came to some islands, some islanders sought out new opportunities abroad. But the region retained its unique combination of European, African, Asian, and Caribbean cultures.

CA2023_Ottowa_Ghost.name: Eastern Ontario
CA2023_Ottowa_Ghost.overview: Large numbers of European settlers came to Ontario when Loyalists fled north after the American Revolution. These early settlers endured backbreaking work, clearing dense forests to create farmland on lands long used or inhabited by Indigenous peoples, who were often displaced through treaties or by force. Their descendants pushed west to the Ottawa River Valley, where they farmed and cut timber, depending on the season. Life got easier as roads, mills, and towns were built, which helped early industries get started. The two world wars sped up Ontario's growth as a manufacturing center, making it Canada's most populous and wealthiest province.

AFAM192021_1.12.name: Central Ohio & Northern West Virginia African Americans
AFAM192021_1.12.overview: Most African Americans in this region are descendants of West Africans brought to America through the transatlantic slave trade. By 1800, slavery shaped life in Virginia, where enslaved people worked on farms, in homes, and as skilled laborers. Even while facing violence and family separation, African Americans built strong communities, kept cultural traditions alive, and resisted slavery. Some escaped to freedom by crossing the Ohio River on the Underground Railroad. Others founded free Black settlements in central Ohio. After the Civil War, Black communities continued to grow through churches, schools, businesses, and neighborhoods despite ongoing racism and discrimination.

MI-MN-WI_MN2024_Ghost.overview: When Europeans arrived in the 1600s, Minnesota was the homeland of the Dakota and Ojibwe nations. French traders brought metal tools and guns but also deadly diseases like smallpox, which killed many Indigenous people. Over time, British and U.S. government policies pushed Indigenous communities off their lands, and migrants from the eastern United States and Germany built communities where generations maintained their languages and traditions. World War I brought prejudice and persecution to the state’s German communities. By the end of World War II, German Minnesotans had become much more assimilated, and towns throughout the region continued to celebrate their cultural heritage.

Mexico_2021_2.5.name: Nacogdoches, Texas to Natchitoches, Louisiana
Mexico_2021_2.5.overview: Most settlers in this community can trace their roots back to England, Scotland, or Mexico/Spain. Early ideas of independence and revolutionary ideals thrived via fierce localism and an ongoing distrust of government authorities and outsiders. Small farms and plantations growing cotton to peanuts dotted the Red River Basin, while logging, drilling, and machining proceeded as well. Riverways and rail lines also made this area a bustling spot for travelers. But the region’s unique cultural heritage is embodied in natural medicine, folktales, flavorful food, and lively music.

LA2023_8.2.name: Costa Rica
LA2023_8.2.overview: Costa Rica’s history reflects the blending of Indigenous cultures, Spanish and English colonizers, and Africans brought through the slave trade. Unlike other countries, Costa Rica had no mineral wealth to exploit, so people farmed to survive. After independence, Costa Rica built its economy on the coffee trade, which created a wealthy class of coffee growers who dominated political and economic life. By the 20th century, the capital city of San José had grown rapidly, with investment in schools, industries, roads, and the arts. Many Costa Ricans moved there for opportunities, while others migrated to Panama and the United States.

FRAM2019_1.1.overview: Early French migrants to New France (modern-day Quebec) came for the fur trade. They soon settled on the banks of the St. Lawrence River and created an agricultural, family-centered, deeply religious folklife in rural Canada. Hard times pushed many French Canadians south toward opportunity in the United States: first to lumber camps and later to vibrant cultural enclaves in industrial cities. There, a distinctly Franco-American culture blossomed, with a firm grasp of their past but an eye to the future.

LA2023_8.3.name: Panama

subjourneys.LA2023_8.3.1: Gulf of Chiriquí & Eastern Gulf of Panama

LA2023_8.3.overview: Panama’s population is a combination of Indigenous peoples and those of European and African heritage. This mix of cultures has been referred to as sancocho, also the name of a popular local stew with many ingredients that each retain their original flavor. Connecting North and South America, the Isthmus of Panama includes mountains, savannas, and thick jungle. The Panama Canal, which opened in 1914, changed the course of the global economy and life for Panamanians then and since.

LA2023_2.2.7.name: Uruguay
LA2023_2.2.7.overview: Beginning in the 1500s, European powers battled for control of trade along the Río de la Plata, an important waterway for shipping livestock products overseas. The nearby Pampas grasslands, with their mild climate, were ideal for cattle ranching, which gave rise to a gaucho (cowboy) culture on both sides of the river. After independence, Uruguay attracted many European immigrants, most of whom settled in Montevideo. The diverse population transformed the capital into a cosmopolitan city that blended European influences with regional traditions.

US_NSC_19th_2019_1.2.7.name: Southern Pennsylvania, Northern Ohio, Indiana & Illinois Settlers
US_NSC_19th_2019_1.2.7.overview: Starting in the 1700s, crop failures, ongoing wars, and poverty drove thousands of Germans and English to make the arduous journey across the Atlantic to find a better life in the New World. Anabaptist farmers from Germany found fertile land and greater religious freedom in the frontier colony of Pennsylvania. Following the turmoil of the American Revolution, these settlers pushed westward into Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois, repeating the patterns of their ancestors in seeking out land, freedom, and new opportunities. However, some Amish stayed in Pennsylvania.

LA2023_Venezuela_Ghost.overview: Venezuela’s varied landscape includes the high Andes Mountains, the tropical jungles of the Amazon, and the sunny beaches of the Caribbean Sea. From this land, its people forged a vibrant national identity from their Indigenous, Spanish, and African roots—a legacy of encounter, conquest, and resilience. Venezuela is rich in natural resources, and Venezuelans have long been highly mobile, moving about the country for work in agriculture, mining, and petroleum. While most are Catholic, they have maintained robust local religious cultures that weave together Catholic, Indigenous, and African beliefs.

After emancipation, many newly freed African Americans hoped to start farms but often were forced into sharecropping. As racism and discrimination continued to grow, some chose to leave the region in search of greater opportunities in the West, the North, and in Southern cities.

A rigid class system kept laborers at the bottom of the socioeconomic ladder and fueled decades of political instability and revolution. After the Industrial Revolution had sufficiently improved transportation and job options, Mexicans of the Mesa Central began emigrating by the tens of thousands. Today their descendants are found across Mexico and the United States.

In the face of discrimination, some African Americans in the region founded “Black towns”; others helped build businesses and neighborhoods like D.C.’s “Black Broadway.” By the time of the civil rights area, Washington, D.C. had become a center of African American power, art, and influence.

NA9_PPR_3.name: Puerto Rico
NA9_PPR_3.overview: Puerto Rico was one of Spain’s last colonies in the New World, but native Puerto Ricans no longer saw themselves as Spanish. The island’s people and culture were a mix of native Taino, African, and Spanish influences. Most Puerto Ricans began the 19th century as farmers, but change was coming. Commercial agriculture would turn farmers into laborers, war would leave the country a U.S. territory, and a devastating hurricane would start an exodus that transplanted Puerto Ricans from New York City to Hawaii.

LA2023_Bolivia_Ghost.overview: Bolivia has nearly 40 recognized ethnic groups, including some of the largest Indigenous populations in the Americas. Its culture is shaped by the historic encounter between Indigenous and European societies, with Spanish, Quechua, Aymara, and other Indigenous languages widely spoken. Bolivians have often been a mobile people, moving from the highlands to the lowlands and from rural areas to cities in search of new opportunities. This history has forged a powerful tradition of resistance to colonialism, social inequality, and economic exploitation.

LA2023_BrazilNorth_Ghost.overview: Portuguese colonists began arriving in northeastern Brazil in the early 1500s and soon turned to producing sugar. These plantations relied on enslaved labor to perform the backbreaking work of cultivating sugarcane. After slavery ended in the 1880s and cities grew, the region came to represent what many consider key aspects of Brazilian identity: the cultural and racial mixing of European, Black, and Indigenous peoples and a spirit of independence.

LA2023_1.4.4.name: Guyana
LA2023_1.4.4.overview: The name “Guyana” comes from an Indigenous word meaning “land of many waters,” an apt description for a country crisscrossed by rivers and waterfalls. Much of Guyana remains covered in dense rainforest. Its diverse population includes descendants of Indigenous peoples, enslaved Africans, and indentured laborers from India, China, and Portugal. English is the official language, but Guyanese Creole, a blend of English, African, Indian, and Amerindian influences, is widely spoken. Colonized first by the Dutch and later by the British, Guyana gained independence in 1966. Today, its rich cultural life reflects a fusion of traditions.

CA2023_EastOntario_Ghost.name: Eastern Ontario & Southwestern Quebec
CA2023_EastOntario_Ghost.overview: Eastern Ontario, at the intersection of major waterways, was occupied by the Haudenosaunee, Anishinaabe, and Algonquin peoples long before the arrival of Europeans. Beginning around 1700, immigration to the region increased significantly. Ports in Cornwall, Brockville, Kingston, and Belleville became key hubs for the import and export of produce, grain, and manufactured goods, facilitating the arrival of European settlers seeking opportunity, Empire Loyalists loyal to the Crown, and formerly enslaved people escaping to freedom through the Underground Railroad. The movement of people and goods spurred economic growth and helped shape the region’s rich cultural mosaic.

Far from home and enslaved with other Africans from diverse ethnic groups, they maintained ties to their heritage while also forming distinct African American cultures. These resilient qualities were crucial when, in the early 19th century, enslaved people from the upper south were sold to deep south states like Georgia and Alabama. Despite forced separation, they built communities, developed faith traditions, and resisted bondage.

US_NSCW_18th_2021_2.1.1.overview: Some of the Immigrants whose families first settled in Virginia in the 18th century did not stay long on the East Coast. Many came from Germany, England, and Scotland, with later groups arriving from Ireland seeking land, independence, and a better future for their descendants. These immigrant groups settled in different parts of the American South, where their experience was shaped by challenging landscapes and conflicts among groups vying for control over land and labor. The 19th and 20th centuries brought wars, an oil boom, and cultural shifts throughout the region.

Together they faced the changes that drought, boom and bust, and war brought to a harsh and beautiful land.

Creole culture evolved as people of French heritage interacted with the Louisiana environment and influences from African, Native American, and Spanish cultures. What resulted is a unique culture with food, music, and history unlike anything outside of Louisiana.

FRAM2019_4.3.overview: The Cajuns are a mix of French-speakers expelled from Nova Scotia in 1755 and French Creoles from Louisiana. Though the French language and Canadian origins are important parts of Cajun identity, the community's strong family bonds, agrarian roots, easy-going attitudes, and traditions were born from their experiences within the United States. The Cajuns are one of the country's older and more distinct ethnic groups and are closely associated with their heartland in Louisiana. Beyond Louisiana, however, Cajun migrants have spread out across the Southeast, Texas, and California.

The newcomers brought trades, know-how, and traditions from their homelands, all of which helped their culture to survive and reemerge after the surges of anti-German sentiment that  emerged during two world wars.

In the centuries that followed, people dealt with independence, revolution, social upheaval, and the growth of industry, but the population remained sparse. Many residents migrated south to Mexico City or north to the United States. Those who stayed contributed to northern Mexico’s distinctive culture, shaped by cattle ranching and the blend of European, African, and Indigenous cultures.

Mexico_2021_1.1.3.overview: Thanks to its fertile land, dense population, and long history of civilization and trade, central Mexico had been a seat of power well before the Spanish Conquest. Three centuries of Spanish colonial rule eventually led to political crisis and independence in 1821. Agriculture dominated much of the economy until the mid-20th century, when rural Mexicans began moving to cities.

AFAM192021_1.13.name: New York & New Jersey African Americans
AFAM192021_1.13.overview: Black Americans had lived in New York and New Jersey when British colonizers settled in the 17th century. By 1700, they represented 15% of New York’s population. Black population growth in later decades came through enslaved laborers from Africa and the West Indies, especially between 1715 and 1774. The U.S. Civil War and European immigration changed life dramatically for Black Americans. Employment and discrimination were constant struggles. Despite these obstacles and others, Black New Yorkers and New Jerseyans created a resilient and vibrant culture that laid a solid foundation for future generations.

LA2023_4.4.name: Honduras
LA2023_4.4.overview: Hondurans have experienced colonization, exploitation, and political strife over the centuries since European arrival. Although the Spanish enjoyed comfortable lives when they weren’t fighting other colonial powers for control of the country’s resources, Indigenous and mestizo (mixed Spanish and Indigenous heritage) people eked out a living with subsistence farming and were forced to work in brutal jobs like logging and mining. In the 20th century, the growing banana industry transformed Honduras, for better and for worse. While many workers fought for better living and labor conditions, others left Central America altogether, often for Louisiana, where they met new challenges and opportunities.

LA2023_2.6.name: Spanish in New Orleans
LA2023_2.6.overview: When Spain took control of New Orleans from 1763 to 1803, it governed a complex city built on Indigenous land and reliant on enslaved African labor. Spanish officials encouraged the immigration of Canary Islanders (Isleños) to serve in the military and establish farms. These newcomers added their unique traditions, architecture, and a deep Catholic faith to the city’s evolving Creole culture. Though Spanish rule was brief, the long-term presence of these communities left a lasting imprint on the unique fabric of New Orleans.

US_NSCW_18th_2021_Ghost_NC_Coast.name: Eastern North Carolina Settlers
US_NSCW_18th_2021_Ghost_NC_Coast.overview: North Carolina’s earliest European settlers were English-Americans from Virginia and new immigrants from England and Germany. During the middle 1700s, many Scots-Irish and German settlers arrived from Pennsylvania. North Carolina had more small family farms than its neighbors to the south. But it also had larger plantations. Tobacco plantations in the Piedmont and Coastal Plain regions used enslaved African labor. After the Civil War, North Carolinians produced tobacco products, textiles, and furniture. Following World War II, the region attracted tourism and technology.

US_NSC_18th_2019_1.3.2.overview: By the turn of the 18th century, Britain’s North American colonies were well established on land purchased from, negotiated for, or fought over with Native Americans or French troops. Puritans had been immigrating to the Massachusetts area since the 1600s, and by the mid 18th century, groups had spread to surrounding areas. Many families stayed in an area for generations and helped turn New England into an industrial powerhouse in the 19th century. Others headed west, spreading the Yankee legacy of hard work, community, and spirituality.

US_NSCW_18th_2021_2.3.1.overview: Starting in the mid-1700s, immigrants of English, Scottish, and German descent left Virginia and headed into modern-day Kentucky and Tennessee. Conflicts arose as they pushed Cherokee, Shawnee, Yuchi, and other Native American nations out to make room for settlements and farms. Life revolved around small farms, salt works, plantations, and river towns until the Civil War. Afterward, coal mines, company towns, and industrial cities drew families away from the land and even their homes. Traditions like family, religion, and music helped them maintain ties to home.

AFAM192021_1.4.3.overview: Haiti occupies the western third of the island of Hispaniola in the Caribbean Sea, sharing a border with the Dominican Republic. The mountainous island has a tumultuous history marked by slavery, rebellion, trade wars, and natural disasters. Nearly 95% of Haiti’s population is of African descent. They speak primarily Haitian Creole. Despite political turmoil and extreme poverty, Haitians continue to seek dignity of life and freedom from outside rule.

KS-TX-UMW-WUS_KS2024_Ghost.overview: Among the earliest and largest groups of immigrants to the American colonies were the Scots-Irish and Germans. Many left their homelands because of poverty, political conflict, and religious persecution. In search of land and better opportunities, they moved west over time, settling in places like Missouri, Kansas, and Colorado. German Americans faced strong prejudice during World Wars I and II, but many communities kept their language, food, and traditions. Both groups played an important role in shaping farming, local government, and daily life in the Midwest, influences that can still be seen today.

subjourneys.LA2023_3.4.3: Southern Manabí, Guayas & Western Los Ríos

LA2023_Ecuador_Ghost.overview: Ecuador is a nation of profound diversity, with roots in Indigenous, European, and African ancestry—a legacy of Spanish conquest and the transatlantic slave trade. Straddling the Equator, its geography ranges from the Pacific coast to the Andean Sierra, where cities like Quito and Cuenca are nestled among volcanoes, and deep into the Amazonian basin. Before the conquest, these regions were home to distinct societies linked by trade. The history that followed was defined by an ongoing struggle over land and labor, met by the resilience and resistance of its diverse communities.

Many of them ended up in the Pennsylvanian, Virginian, and Carolinian backcountry. As they continued west, these farmers settled Central Appalachia where the steep, timbered mountains provided a unique challenge to survival. The discovery of coal transformed the region into a network of mining towns whose success often fluctuated between boom and bust.

AFAM192021_1.4.5.name: Bahamas
AFAM192021_1.4.5.overview: Black Bahamians have roots in West African countries from the Ivory Coast to the Congo. Until the 19th century, the Bahamas participated in piracy, privateering, and the slave trade. The population remained small until the arrival of British Loyalists after the American Revolution. The end of the British slave trade further swelled the population with newly freed Africans. But with limited natural resources, the islands offered few long-term economic opportunities, and Bahamians began emigrating in large numbers at the beginning of the 20th century.

While some descendants amassed great wealth, others survived by serving the wealthy. Fortunes began to turn with the California Gold Rush, which diminished Hispanic influence and began a new era of racial discrimination. Despite hardships, descendants of the original settlers have made California their home for centuries.

CA2023_NovaScotia_Ghost.name: Nova Scotia

CA2023_NovaScotia_Ghost.overview: The Mi’kmaq people were the first to call Nova Scotia home. The French began settling Nova Scotia in the 17th century. English-speaking settlement began in the early 18th century with fortified villages and ports for trading. British immigrants displaced the local Mi’kmaq and French, cleared rocky plots for farming, and hunted fish, seals, and crustaceans off the coast. Transplanted Scots helped create a mid-19th-century working class that labored in mines and mills. Over time, residents balanced folk traditions and modern conveniences. They also travelled to New England and throughout Canada in search of opportunities and connections.

AFAM182021_1.6.overview: The first enslaved Africans trafficked to the Lower Mississippi Valley arrived in French Louisiana in 1719. Over time, they labored on rice, indigo, cotton, and sugar plantations, as well as in skilled labor and domestic service positions in cities. With the arrival of the Americans in the early 19th-century, slavery intensified and hundreds of thousands were subject to brutal conditions. After the Civil War, many African Americans and Creoles became sharecroppers and independent wage laborers, but they continued to suffer racial violence and oppression. By the 1930s, many looked for greater freedom and prosperity by moving to cities like New York, Chicago, Houston, and Los Angeles.

Mexico_2021_1.3.2_1.3.4_Ghost.overview: The Mexican state of Sinaloa has long been a cultural crossroads. Before the Spanish arrived in the 1500s, it was populated by at least a dozen Indigenous groups who had been in contact with one another but still preserved their diverse cultures. Chinese and German immigrants came later and added their own influence on Sinaloan culinary and music traditions. Today, Sinaloa has retained its nickname as “the Breadbasket of Mexico” for its production of staple grains and vegetables, but it’s also famous for its seafood and beloved banda music that has come to represent all of northwestern Mexico.

AFAM192021_1.11.name: Robeson County, North Carolina, Lumbee & African Americans
AFAM192021_1.11.overview:
Robeson County, North Carolina—where the Lumber River flows—has long been the center for the Lumbee Tribe. Archeological evidence indicates a continuous Indigenous presence there for at least 14,000 years. The Lumbee descend from this ancestral population, as well as from Eastern Siouan, Iroquoian, and Algonquian-speaking refugees and African Maroons who formed a growing community in the North Carolina swamps as more enslaved Africans were brought to North Carolina. Together they were able to survive European colonization, warfare, and enslavement.

Generation after generation, they protected and cared for their families and communities, leaving behind monuments both seen and unseen.

In late colonial times, families of English, German, and Scots-Irish ancestry began settling the hill country west of the Piedmont, where they encountered Native peoples, including the Monacan and Shawnee. The diversity of the immigrant population and the demands of their new lives forged a distinct culture. When Virginia seceded from the Union in 1861, the “Mountaineers” in the western counties found a way to secede from Virginia, creating their own state in 1863. Loggers, coal miners, and industrial workers from this area fueled America’s industrial and military might into the 20th century.

LA2023_8.1.overview: Despite being Central America’s largest country, Nicaragua is relatively sparsely populated. It spans volcanic highlands, tropical rainforests, grassy plains, and two massive lakes. Nicaraguans claim a mix of European (primarily Spanish), Indigenous, and African ancestry. They celebrate their diverse heritage through music, dance, and festivals. Traditional foods include gallo pinto (rice and beans), güirila (sweet-corn tortillas), and a drink of toasted cornmeal and cacao called pinolillo. The drink earned Nicaraguans the nickname Pinoleros, although they’re also commonly called Nicas.

This led settlers to migrate west into the Ohio River Valley as the U.S. government pushed more Native Americans from their lands. First farms, then factories developed along the river, along with railways, highways, and canals. Over time, the region developed a culture known for diversity, industry, and hope.

Mexico_2021_2.1.overview: Because politics and war kept shifting the border between the U.S. and Mexico, populations in Texas and Mexico share an intertwined history that has endured centuries of change. Watered by the Rio Grande, the original Indigenous and Spanish settlements grew into robust hacienda economies. Later they became an industrialized crossroads that links the United States and Mexico to the world, thanks to some important port cities. Texas and northeast Mexico’s enduring cultural contributions include unique foods, clothing, music, and worldviews that continue to shape the region.

US_NSC_18th_2019_1.2.1.name: Delaware Valley, Chesapeake & Midwest Settlers
US_NSC_18th_2019_1.2.1.overview: The Chesapeake Bay and Delaware River valleys were popular destinations for colonial migrants from England, Scotland, and German-speaking territories. Searching for a good place to farm, many descendants of these people followed the Great Wagon Road south into Virginia’s backcountry. The drive for economic opportunity also fueled westward migration to the Midwest and ended in California in the 20th century. These Americans usually migrated in family and community groups and established new settlements across the country.

subjourneys.LA2023_9.1.4: Santiago | Jarabacoa | San Francisco de Macoris

LA2023_9.overview: The Dominican people represent a blend of Taíno, West African, and European heritage. Spain took control of eastern Hispaniola in the late 1400s, while France ruled the west. Colonization devastated the Taíno through disease, forced labor, and loss of land, yet their influence survived in language, farming techniques, food, and place names. Colonial life centered on small farms and crops like sugar, tobacco, coffee, and cacao, which tied the colony to Caribbean and Atlantic trade. Over time, through resistance, alliances, and work, Dominicans shaped a distinct identity reflected in their food, love of baseball, and strong traditions of public and community life.

Mexico_2021_1.4.overview: Modern-day Jalisco, Colima, and Michoacán’s central location, natural resources, and mix of farmland and coastline created a geography of plenty where cultures developed and flourished. Before the Spanish conquest, this region was home to many Indigenous groups, including the Huichol, Cora, and the vast Purépecha (Tarascan) Empire. Spanish colonists raised the corn and livestock that fueled the mining industry in the 18th and 19th centuries. It was a hotbed of revolution and the birthplace of Mexican cultural staples like tequila, mariachi, and ranchera music.

CA2023_Ontario_Ghost.overview: The lucrative fur and timber trade sparked the settlement and growth of Southern Ontario, along with its rich soils for farming, opportunities for social mobility, religious and political freedoms, and access to trade and business markets. Ontario has been at the crossroads for centuries for those seeking freedom and prosperity. Through the long St. Lawrence Seaway and Great Lakes, along the extensive railroads, and by way of highways and skyways, Ontario has become a hub of industry, trade, and migration. It has long been a place of both opportunity and struggle for immigrants and the Indigenous peoples whose lands and cultures continue to shape the province.

One of the most important events is the annual pilgrimage to Caacupé, where thousands honor the Virgin of Caacupé, Paraguay’s patron saint.

US_NSC_18th_2019_1.2.2.name: Early Pennsylvania Settlers
US_NSC_18th_2019_1.2.2.overview: English Quakers founded Pennsylvania as a bastion of religious freedom and tolerance. Thousands of German and Swiss Mennonites, Anabaptists, Anglicans, and Scottish Presbyterians followed, drawn by the promise of religious freedom and acres of rich farmland. Their industry and success raised Pennsylvania to prominence among the American colonies. Their soldiers helped ensure a Union victory in the Civil War, and they went on to leave their stamp on the settling and culture of the American Midwest.

They brought enslaved Africans to labor on plantations and farms, and expansion also led to the forcible removal of Indigenous nations like the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Creeks. US_NSC_19th_Ghost_MD_DE.overview: The Chesapeake Bay region, which encompasses Maryland and parts of Virginia, Delaware, and Pennsylvania, was one of the earliest sites of English colonization in America. During colonial times, colonists who grew tobacco flourished by creating large plantations that exploited enslaved laborers, a practice that continued after independence. Over time, farmers diversified away from tobacco, and Baltimore developed as a major port. This strong economic base was a draw for migrants from Europe because factories and farms offered good jobs.

US_NSCW_19th_2021_Ghost_NC.name: North Carolina Settlers
US_NSCW_19th_2021_Ghost_NC.overview: The 18th-century settlers of North Carolina’s central Piedmont and western counties were primarily Scots-Irish and German migrants. Most came from Pennsylvania and the Mid-Atlantic by following the Great Wagon Road, a former Native American trading trail. English migrants from Virginia also settled in the state, often in the eastern portions. The central and western regions tended to have small family farms and fewer enslaved people than farther south, making the culture and economy distinct from Coastal North Carolina. In the 19th and 20th centuries, the region became a leading center for textiles, furniture, handicrafts, and technology.

FRAM2019_1.2.name: Southeastern Quebec French Settlers
FRAM2019_1.2.overview: Among the earliest settlers in North America, the French Canadians have long been associated with the woods and rural spaces. Early migrants to New France (modern-day Quebec) came for the fur trade. They soon settled on the banks of the St. Lawrence River. From there, some moved to rural New England and Michigan in search of work in timbering and pulp and paper. They became renowned for their prowess and carved a place for themselves in the rural North while combating both ethnic prejudice and nature.

They traveled along rivers to trade with Indigenous nations and relied on alliances with them to survive harsh winters. Many married Indigenous women, forming Métis families shaped by blended cultural traditions. Even as they adapted, they kept their French language, Catholic faith, and strong family ties. French trading posts later grew into cities such as Detroit, Green Bay, St. Louis, and Chicago. Today, place names, surnames, and descendants across the Midwest still reflect this early French influence.

LA2023_ColombiaWest_Ghost.overview: Over hundreds of years, Indigenous peoples, Spanish colonists, and Africans (originally brought as enslaved laborers) all contributed to Western Colombia’s unique and diverse culture and population. Independence from Spain brought little change to the daily lives of most Colombians at first. Society was divided by class, and most people remained poor. Many were isolated by the country’s mountainous terrain, and local loyalties typically trumped national ones. This history forged a region of resilient local cultures, but one defined by a long and often violent struggle between its immense natural wealth and deep-seated social inequality.

Once there, they typically worked on farms or plantations, growing everything from cotton to hemp. After emancipation, they built and attended schools, started farms and businesses, and looked forward to participating in civic life. Faced with Jim Crow restrictions and limited economic opportunities, many left the South in the early 20th century.

Over time, these communities blended European traditions with new American ideas, shaping a Midwestern identity based on hard work, cooperation, and steady growth from prairie land into farming regions and towns.

Settlers faced the challenges of homesteading on the frontier, cholera epidemics, violent conflicts with Indigenous peoples over land and resources, disputes over slavery, and ethnic persecution. Through it all, Midwesterners developed thriving cultural communities as they ventured all the way to the Pacific.

LA2023_Cuba_Ghost.overview: Spain colonized Cuba for nearly four centuries, devastating the Indigenous Taíno population, though Taíno heritage endured. Centuries of the transatlantic slave trade also made Cuba a center of African culture, profoundly shaping its music, religion, and society. The island’s economy was defined by small tobacco farms and vast sugar plantations, where the labor of enslaved people generated immense wealth. The long struggle for independence forged a unique national identity from these influences. Cuba is a cultural crossroads, known for its vibrant music, dance, and cuisine—some of the nation’s greatest exports.

LA2023_Argentina_Ghost.name: Argentina
LA2023_Argentina_Ghost.overview: Argentina’s culture developed from many influences. Indigenous peoples lived in the area for centuries before Spanish colonization changed their way of life. In the late 1800s and early 1900s, waves of immigrants arrived, especially from Italy and Spain, bringing their own traditions. Out of these different and sometimes conflicting histories, Argentina created a unique national identity. This identity can be seen in the tango, the country’s deep love for soccer, and its rich tradition of literature and art, all of which continue to shape modern Argentina.

LA2023_4.1.overview: The Indigenous peoples of Guatemala have a rich history, culture, and language. Their ancestors developed the concept of zero and a sophisticated system of writing. Though Spanish colonizers and later governments seized their land and imposed systems of forced labor, Indigenous peoples persevered through their own farming, weaving, and healing traditions. This history has forged a nation defined by the profound resilience of its Maya majority in the face of persistent inequality and political conflict.

US_NSCW_19th_2021_1.7.1.name: Upper Midwest & Western U.S. Settlers
US_NSCW_19th_2021_1.7.1.overview: After arriving in the Middle Colonies during the 1700s, English, Irish, and German settlers pushed westward into the Ohio River Valley and southward into the Carolinas in search of prosperity. European colonists and the United States removed Indigenous nations such as the Shawnee, Cherokee, Chickasaw, Creek, Miami, and Delaware through warfare, land seizures, and unfair treaties. After the American Revolution, migrants moved into Kentucky, Tennessee, and the Old Northwest, building farms and towns along major rivers. The Ohio and Mississippi Rivers—and later canals and railroads—helped transport Midwestern crops and livestock to markets across the growing United States.

AFAM192021_1.4.1_Ghost.overview: Jamaica is a mountainous, lush island flanked by white sand beaches. The diverse topography attracted Spanish and then British colonizers. They cultivated a variety of crops on its plains and grew coffee in the mountains. The ancestors of Jamaicans who were of African descent were torn from their lives in West Africa, enslaved, and brought to work on British sugar plantations. Jamaicans have a rich history of cultural expression and resistance. The home of reggae and Rastafarianism, Jamaica is now a cultural hub of the Afro-Caribbean world.

US_NSC_18th_2019_1.3.1.overview: Famine and economic hardship in much of England and Germany caused many to flee to the United States. They were drawn to small villages on the East Coast, finding work in fishing, agriculture, and shipbuilding. Eventually, many moved to urban centers like New York City and Albany. The Erie Canal and later the railroad opened up even more opportunities. Immigrants settled in Michigan, Seattle, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. Everywhere they went, the immigrants left their mark because of their work ethic and innovative spirit.

During the 18th century, colonial settlement expanded rapidly, and the Carolinas split into North and South. Most of the people enslaved in North Carolina worked on small farms, though some practiced trades. A small minority of enslaved Africans gained or purchased their freedom. Others escaped to form the largest community of American Maroons, living alongside Indigenous refugees in the Great Dismal Swamp.

Newcomers planted and harvested everything from tobacco to soybeans, trying to survive and thrive. Descendants of these settlers created an enduring culinary heritage based on simple but flavorful foods. The great value they placed on family, faith, storytelling, and love of the land remains a hallmark of this unique culture.

CA2018_594.64.name: Cardston, Alberta Mormon Pioneers

As the territory’s irrigable farmland became scarce and LDS polygamists came under pressure from the U.S. government to cease practicing plural marriage, many Saints moved to southern Alberta, Canada in search of economic success and religious freedom.

Strains of fundamentalist religion, frontier influences, and Southern cotton culture all helped shape the region as we know it today.

LA2023_RhodeIsland_Ghost.name: Portuguese Islanders in the Eastern United States
LA2023_RhodeIsland_Ghost.overview: The Portuguese and Cape Verdean presence in Rhode Island began in the mid-1800s with whaling ships. While often grouped together, these communities had distinct origins: Azoreans were European, while Cape Verdeans were a Creole people of West African and Portuguese heritage. However, by the early 19th century, the islands couldn’t support their growing populations. To escape poverty, many men joined crews on American whaling ships, and families eventually made their way to towns on the East Coast of the U.S.

AFAM182021_1.7.overview: Located between the Chesapeake Bay and the Atlantic Ocean, the Delmarva Peninsula is divided among the states of Delaware, Maryland, and Virginia. The western side of the peninsula is often called the Eastern Shore, and Delaware occupies much of the eastern side. Before the Civil War, this region played an important role in the plantation economy. It represented both abolitionist and slaveholder mentalities. Because of this diversity, the experiences of people of color on the peninsula varied widely. By the 1900s, the peninsula’s culture shared more in common with the South than with the Mid-Atlantic states.

US_NSCW_18th_2021_2.3.3.overview: Starting in the mid-1700s, immigrants of English, Scots-Irish, and German descent left a crowded Virginia colony and pushed into Kentucky territory. Conflicts over land followed, and the new settlers violently pushed Native Americans, including the Cherokee, out of the state in their march westward. Early settlers farmed or found jobs at salt works or in river towns. Coal mining became a way of life in Appalachia in the late 19th century. Appalachians started leaving Kentucky in the early 20th century, taking their culture and traditions with them.

CA2023_1.5.overview: In the 18th century, British immigrants began settling in present-day New Brunswick in areas long inhabited by Indigenous peoples like the Mi'kmaq and Wolastoqiyik. While river valleys offered good farmland, the cool climate and generally hilly terrain were unsuited to large-scale agriculture. However, the fish-rich waters and abundant forests, traditionally used by Indigenous nations, drew European investment. Most Anglo-New Brunswickers were Protestants, with Irish and Scottish Catholics forming a minority. Settler livelihoods included farming, logging, fishing, and trade, industries whose fluctuations spurred migrations to locations in New England and across Canada.

US_NSCW_19th_2021_1.7.56.overview: After the murder of their prophet, Joseph Smith, and his brother in Carthage, Illinois, members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (or Mormons) trekked more than a thousand miles across the plains to settle the Utah territory, escaping religious persecution and financial hardship. Many of these settlers were European immigrants from countries like England and Scotland. Conversion to Mormonism as well as mining, railroads, and Utah’s natural beauty would continue to attract thousands from all over the world to migrate to Utah and settle there.

Influenced by their religious backgrounds, they emphasized community and education wherever they moved.

LA2023_Beliz_Ghost.name: Belize
LA2023_Beliz_Ghost.overview: While most of Central America came under Spanish rule, the area now known as Belize remained largely outside Spain’s control. By the 17th century, English settlers established logging camps along the coast, harvesting valuable hardwoods like mahogany. Spain repeatedly tried to expel the British over the centuries, but the English remained dominant. Known as British Honduras, the colony relied on timber exports and later expanded into agriculture. Although Indigenous and Afro-descendant laborers faced exploitation and inequality, political life was relatively stable. Belize achieved self-government in 1964 and full independence in 1981.

Today, the country is primarily Roman Catholic and of mixed heritage. Before Spanish colonization in the 16th century, it was inhabited by Indigenous peoples. After gaining independence from Spain in 1821, El Salvador endured decades of political instability, including a devastating civil war from 1980 to 1992 that resulted in significant displacement and loss of life. However, the country maintains strong cultural traditions.

Mexico_2021_1.1.4.overview: Thanks to its fertile land, dense population, and long history of civilization and trade, central Mexico was a seat of power well before the Spanish Conquest. The Mexica, or Aztecs, expanded their power throughout central Mexico and as far south as Oaxaca, forcing Indigenous peoples under their rule to pay tribute. In Mexico City, the Spanish Empire established its administrative center, imposing a rigid race and class system that kept Indigenous, Black, and multiracial laborers at the bottom of the social and economic ladder and brought wealth and power to the Spanish settlers and their descendants.

MENA2023_2.5.name: Sephardic Jews of North Africa
MENA2023_2.5.overview: The Jews of North Africa have been an integral part of the region’s cultural fabric for millennia. They helped build important trade centers, and many gained favor and high-ranking positions in the administration of the Ottoman Empire. Some lived in separate, walled Jewish neighborhoods called mellahs, while others lived among Muslims, sharing traditional foods and music. European colonization in the 19th century caused an upheaval in the lives of all North Africans, and many waves of Jewish emigration took place both during and after World War II, in response to the creation of the state of Israel in 1948.

CA2023_1.4.16.name: Prince Edward Island
CA2023_1.4.16.overview: British settlement of Prince Edward Island (PEI) began in the early 18th century, as officials looked to displace the native Mi’kmaq and French living on the island. At less than 140 miles long, PEI emerged as an important stop for Atlantic maritime traffic. Highland Scots and displaced Irish emigrants settled across the island, bringing Catholic influences and farming knowledge. By the 1900s, many islanders left for jobs elsewhere in Canada and New England, while others stayed behind, preserving the unique PEI lifestyle.

AFAM192021_1.1.2.overview: Many African Americans in this community trace their roots back to West Africa, where for centuries white enslavers bought men, women, and children and brought them to labor in the Americas. Arriving in Texas and Oklahoma in the early 1800s, most worked on cotton plantations or small family farms. After emancipation, many African Americans worked their own small farms as sharecroppers or in the booming lumber industry. And when the chance came in the early 20th century, thousands left to make new homes in western or northern industrial cities.

ASIA2023_1.3.8.name: Southeast India
ASIA2023_1.3.8.overview: As the Tamil and Telugu speakers of South India navigated British colonialism, they also considered how their society, languages, and religious life should function. South Indians found some refuge in their culture. They crafted music and literature that took stock of and reimagined their longer histories, even as they debated what new ideas or religions might be meaningful to them. By the 1900s, the region was emerging as a distinct political center in India’s fight for independence. After independence, the newly established states provided Tamil and Telugu speakers new opportunities to develop their politics, literature, and language.

AFAM192021_1.5.overview: Most African Americans in this community can trace their ancestry back to West Africa, though many came by way of the West Indies, where they had also been enslaved. Though a few Black Carolinians were free before the Civil War, the majority worked as enslaved laborers on small farms or plantations. After emancipation, Jim Crow laws and racial violence prompted hundreds of thousands to move north. United by family, community, and religious ties, both those who left and those who stayed in the Carolinas fought for equality and an end to segregation.

MENA2023_3.3.name: Western Levant
MENA2023_3.3.overview: The Western Levant was home to diverse groups of mostly Arabic-speaking peoples, including members of various Christian, Jewish and Muslim sects. Before the Ottoman Empire collapsed after World War I, emigrants from the area were typically called “Syrians” or “Turks.” Like other ethnic communities who immigrated to the United States, Syrians came to work in an America desperate for laborers, where they could make money and then return home to live a comfortable life—though many ended up staying and forging a new life there.

MI-MN-WI_MI2024_Ghost.overview: Long before Europeans arrived, the lands that became Michigan were the homeland of diverse Indigenous nations, including the Anishinaabe. By the 1700s, French and British fur traders established outposts, often relying on Indigenous alliances. Later in the century, English and German migrants arrived, clearing fields on seized land. Over time, Michigan became known for its auto plants, lumber camps, and mining towns fueled by immigrant, Black, and Indigenous labor. After long workdays, Michiganders embraced the outdoors, filling their free time with baseball, fishing, concerts, and summer picnics.

MENA2023_1.3.name: Anatolian Turks
MENA2023_1.3.overview: Anatolia, the geographical designation for the land mass occupied by Türkiye (Turkey), has been home to Turkish peoples since migrations from the East in the 11th century. Already home to a diversity of peoples, the Turks added their unique culture and language. Having adopted Islam under Ottoman rulership, they conquered the Byzantine Empire and made Constantinople (Istanbul) their capital. Originally nomadic, Turks settled in towns and cities across the former Byzantine land and developed a great urban culture. The result was a hybrid culture, comprising the most colorful aspects of its many constituents.

ASIA2023_1.3.5.name: Goans
ASIA2023_1.3.5.overview: The Portugese-Indian community, rooted in Goa but with a presence across India and later the world, developed a unique culture that blended Portuguese Catholic and coastal Indian elements. Throughout several centuries of imperial conquest and resistance, the Goan mestiço (“mixed”) community bridged cultures in religious and cultural life, even as Goans’ desires for cultural and political independence grew. In the 20th century, many in the Goan community moved to other places within India, to Portugal, to East Africa, and to England.

ASIA2023_1.4.2.name: Thailand
ASIA2023_1.4.2.overview: Thailand is home to diverse ethnic groups that extend beyond the boundaries of the modern nation. Beginning in the late 1800s, the government introduced reforms to assimilate the land’s diverse peoples into a single, recognizable Thai culture, promoting its language, cuisine, and Buddhist values. By the mid-20th century, rice production, international trade, and manufacturing were well-established industries when tourism and service sectors gained prominence. These developments, among others, contributed to Bangkok becoming one of the most populous cities in the region.

ASIA2023_1.1.3.name: Okinawa
ASIA2023_1.1.3.overview: Okinawa is the best known and largest island in the Ryukyu chain, located south of Japan and east of China. From the 1600s onward, local populations grew sweet potatoes and sugar cane, participating in a global market with China and Japan through tribute and trade. After being annexed by the Japanese in 1879, Okinawans fought to maintain their own culture amidst pressure to assimilate. With the turn of the century, many left, hoping for employment and safety in mainland Japan or the Hawaiian Islands, where strong Okinawan communities continue today.

AFAM-IL-OHIN_IL2024_Ghost.overview: Many Native nations lived across the land that would later become Illinois, including Cahokias, Kaskaskias, Peorias, and others. Together they formed a loose confederation known as the Illinois or Illiniwek. In the late 18th and early 19th centuries, newcomers began moving into the region from several directions. Some migrants arrived from Europe, while many others came from nearby states such as Pennsylvania, Kentucky, Ohio, Tennessee, and Virginia in search of farmland, mining work, or other opportunities. Over time, railroads, canals, and expanding markets tied the region more closely to the rest of the country. Although cities like Chicago grew into major commercial hubs, much of Illinois remained rural, shaped by farm life, migration, immigrant communities, and local politics.

AFAM192021_1.4.6_1.4.7_Ghost.name: Afro-Caribbean Peoples of Belize, Honduras & Nicaragua

subjourneys.AFAM192021_1.4.7: Bay Islands to Coastal Honduras, & Nicaraguan South Caribbean Coast

AFAM192021_1.4.6_1.4.7_Ghost.overview: The lowland tropical forests of the Caribbean coast of Belize, Honduras, and Nicaragua are home to two peoples who have African ancestry: Creoles and Garifuna (Garinagu). The Creoles (Kriols) have mixed African and European ancestry. Many of their ancestors were brought to Belize, Honduras, and Nicaragua as indentured servants or as enslaved workers from the West Indies, mainly from Jamaica and the Cayman Islands. The Garifuna people descend from escaped enslaved Africans and the indigenous Kalingo-Taino (Carib-Arawak) people from the island of Saint Vincent.

US_NSCW_18th_2021_2.1.3.overview: Originating in the British Isles and Germany, these colonists took part in some of the largest human migrations in U.S. history. They had a gnawing appetite for land and were willing to face great risks to get it. Arriving from Europe, they settled in what was then the Southern Backcountry, east of the Blue Ridge Mountains. After the Revolutionary War, they settled throughout Tennessee and Kentucky before moving on to Oklahoma and Texas.

MENA2023_1.1.name: Eastern Anatolia & Armenia
MENA2023_1.1.overview: While many may think of the small Caucasian Republic of Armenia as the homeland of the Armenian people, eastern Turkey, with its high plateaus and mountainous terrain, was the heartland of the Armenian nation for millennia. The Armenians prospered for centuries under Islamic Ottoman rule despite being a Christian minority. Hope for a better life and escape from oppression and genocide led the majority of Armenians to flee their homeland in eastern Turkey in the early 20th century.
