US_NSCW_18th_2021_2.1.4.overview: The southern Appalachia Mountains shaped the peoples who inhabited them. Both the bounties and the scarcities profoundly influenced the region’s history, culture, and economy. In late colonial times, groups of predominantly British and German immigrants traveled south from Pennsylvania along the Great Wagon Road to western Virginia, some bringing enslaved Africans with them. In succeeding generations, they pressed farther south and west, seeking better land and opportunity. They frequently clashed with Native Americans until the U.S. government forcibly removed the Native Peoples from the land.

MENA2023_Iran_Ghost.name: Iran
MENA2023_Iran_Ghost.overview: From the powerful Safavid Empire to the modern-day Islamic Republic, Iran’s history is as diverse as its landscape. Peoples from Central Asia, the Caucasus, and the Arabian Peninsula all made homes in Persia, a name initially attributed to the region by the Greeks. The nation’s mosaic of religious and ethnic communities all contributed to the nation's rich cultural heritage. The 20th century brought significant changes with the discovery of oil, the Constitutional Revolution, the rise of nationalism, and modernization. These changes set the stage for the Iranian Revolution of 1979.

ASIA2023_1.3.16.name: Sri Lanka
ASIA2023_1.3.16.overview: The culture of Sri Lanka, previously known as Ceylon, was shaped by Dutch and Portuguese traders and missionaries who arrived in search of spices like cinnamon and pepper. The British later brought new infrastructure to Sri Lanka but also implemented the harsh working conditions of plantation farming for crops like coffee and tea. All the while, Sinhalese speakers drew strength from ancient epics and Buddhist religious traditions, while Tamil speakers brought Hindu practices to the plantations where they worked. But the tensions between these groups remained after independence. The island’s Sinhalese and Tamil populations clashed, culminating in a civil war.

ASIA2023_2.1.3_2.1.6_Ghost.name: Calabarzon & Manila
ASIA2023_2.1.3_2.1.6_Ghost.overview: On the Philippine island of Luzon, Manila has long been a vital trading and political hub. Growing trade networks helped Luzon’s southern provinces become major sugar, coffee, and rice producers. But the region faced big changes—from the rise and fall of agricultural estates to the upheavals of peasant revolts and World War II to post-independence communist insurgencies. Southern Luzon, however, also became the industrial backdoor of Manila from the 1960s.  This partly explains the resilience of southern Luzon's inhabitants, who adapt to change while still keeping their distinct regional cultures.

ASIA2023_4.6.name: Gujarat
ASIA2023_4.6.overview: The people of Gujarat, skilled craftspeople and traders, have long been used to diversity and change. Long before British rule, merchants worked across religious lines in the service of textile production and trade. Hindu traders calculated profits alongside Muslim, Jain, and Parsi partners in bustling port cities. Some sent their sons to English schools while building textile empires. Factory workers, by the late 19th century, left their villages to work in cotton mills in cities. In the 20th century, Gujarat’s reputation grew linked to the most famous Gujarati, Mohandas Gandhi, whose leadership of India’s independence movement was funded by Gujarati merchants and businessmen.

MENA2023_2.3.name: Sephardic Jews in the Eastern Mediterranean
MENA2023_2.3.overview: “Sephardic” comes from the Hebrew word Sefarad, meaning “Spain,” reflecting the community’s medieval roots in the Iberian kingdoms of Spain and Portugal. They lived there for centuries until the Spanish Inquisition required them to convert to Catholicism, leave Spain, or face execution. Those who left sought refuge in nearly every corner of the Mediterranean, but it was in the Ottoman Empire that they received the warmest welcome. As the Ottoman Empire crumbled, Sephardic Jews were on the move again. Most settled in the Americas, looking for new economic opportunities.

ASIA2023_2.3.name: Central & Eastern Visayas
ASIA2023_2.3.overview: People, products, and politics circulated through the islands of the Visayas and Mindanao. Migrant entrepreneurs, laborers, and farmers traveled to the islands of Panay, Negros, Cebu, Bohol, Leyte, and to and from Mindanao to make money and access land. Early groups worked in concert with the natural environment, providing farmed harvests and forest commodities that connected locals to domestic and international markets. Anti-colonialism was a marked feature of the area, and longstanding resistance to foreign incursion is a powerful dimension of Visayan history.

MENA2023_2.4.name: Mizrahi Jews of Iraq & Iran
MENA2023_2.4.overview: Mizrahi Jews (“Eastern” Jews in Hebrew) were originally brought as exiles to Babylon in the 6th century BCE. Under Cyrus the Great, Jews were permitted to return to the land of Israel. Most, however, chose to remain in the Persian Empire (Iran), and Jewish communities appeared throughout Iran and Central Asia. Eventually they established vast trade networks between these regions, India, and the West. Jews were an indispensable part of the administrative and economic fabric of the region until the mid-20th century, when most Iraqi Jews were forced to emigrate to the new state of Israel.

MENA2023_1.5.name: Northern Iraq & Iran
MENA2023_1.5.overview: The Assyrian Empire was at its height over three millennia ago, but members of this community trace their roots back to the people of that time. Traditionally a tightly-knit community, they have been known variously as Nestorians, Jacobites, Chaldeans, Syriacs, Arameans, or Assyrians. Each of these names refers to people of the same overall ethnic group who adhered to different Christian denominations. Upheaval in their original homelands in northern Iran and Iraq and eastern Turkey created a diaspora whose geographic spread has not diluted their sense of pride and continuity.

ASIA2023_1.3.1.4.name: Parsis in India
ASIA2023_1.3.1.4.overview:
Overview

The Parsis of India follow the Zoroastrian religion of ancient Persia, founded by the Prophet Zarathustra (2nd millennium BCE). They descended from Iranian refugees who fled religious persecution and migrated to western India (around the 9th century). Parsis have assimilated well into Indian society while preserving their distinct religion and customs. Parsis understand the universe to be locked in a struggle between good and evil, light and darkness. The three-fold asha (path) of their faith includes good thoughts, good words, and good deeds. The faithful must choose the good, which will prevail in the end.

ASIA2023_2.1.2_2.1.4_Ghost.name: Central Luzon & North Central Calabarzon

subjourneys.ASIA2023_2.1.4: Eastern Central Luzon & Central & Northern Calabarzon

ASIA2023_2.1.2_2.1.4_Ghost.overview: On the Philippine island of Luzon, the corridor from Pampanga through Manila to Cavite played a pivotal role in the island’s development. Agriculture evolved from subsistence farming to large sugar and rice estates, while towns along Manila Bay developed into industrial and military centers. The corridor's strategic location made it a focal point during major conflicts—from the Philippine Revolution against Spain, through the American colonial period, to the Japanese occupation during World War II. Despite hardships, the region rebuilt repeatedly, emerging as the country's most urbanized and industrialized zone.

MENA2023_3.1_3.2_3.4_Ghost.name: Lebanon

subjourneys.MENA2023_3.2.1.2: Southern Mount Lebanon & Northern South Lebanon

MENA2023_3.1_3.2_3.4_Ghost.overview: Modern Lebanon emerged as an independent country after World War II, following the withdrawal of France, which had controlled the area since the end of World War I. Prior to French occupation of the region, Mount Lebanon was, during four hundred years of Ottoman rule, a province of Greater Syria. Its rulers enjoyed some autonomy in return for keeping order and providing tax revenues and armed men as required by the Ottoman sultan. The area also had a sizable Christian population and a culture with long exposure to Europe.

ASIA2023_1.2.1.name: Eastern & Southeastern China
ASIA2023_1.2.1.overview: Separated by high mountains from the rest of China, the Pearl River Delta has long been known for its independent spirit. Guangzhou, also known as Canton, has been a bustling trade center for centuries, receiving foreign visitors from around the world for nearly a millennium. This independence and international exposure also spurred emigrants to seek their fortunes elsewhere. From Hawai'i to Jamaica, Chinese immigrants from the Pearl River Delta took their culture, cuisine, architecture, and influence with them as they made new lives and new homes.

ASIA2023_4.9.name: Punjabi & Sindhi Hindu
ASIA2023_4.9.overview: The Hindus of Northwest India—primarily in Punjab and Sindh—were caught up in major changes in the 1880s to the 1950s. Connected by language and religion, Punjabi and Sindhi Hindus worked to define religious boundaries and relationships with neighboring communities, primarily Muslims and Sikhs. Language, for many Hindus, played a crucial role, with some Punjabi Hindus supporting Hindi as a marker of national identity. The partition of India in 1947 marked a turning point. Many Punjabi Hindus were forced to leave West Punjab for the new Republic of India. This exodus led to displacement and loss, alongside opportunities to build community and economic strength in independent India.

ASIA2023_AdmixedIndia_Ghost.name: Anglo-Indians
ASIA2023_AdmixedIndia_Ghost.overview: Anglo-Indians largely descended from the merchants who arrived in India from the British Isles, beginning in the 1600s, as employees of or contractors for the East India Company. They emerged as a distinct population on the Indian subcontinent in the following centuries. Their social customs, cuisine, and dress reflected their complex relationship with Indian culture. Initially, they held Indian culture in high regard and took inspiration from it. But they grew more conflicted about integrating with it. By the 19th century, the descendants of British men and Indian women were a uniquely mixed society, both part of Indian society and in some ways separate from it.

LA2023_2.2.10.name: Spanish in the Philippines
LA2023_2.2.10.overview: Spanish colonization in the Felipinas began in 1565, but for the next 200 years, it was of little economic value for the Spanish empire, save as a transhipment port of the China-Mexico galleon trade. This partly explains why most Spaniards in the Philippines lived in Manila, whose center was the walled city of Intramuros (“inside the walls”). The Spaniards who lived outside of Manila were members of the religious orders sent to evangelize towns and villages. It was through them that Spanish influence on Filipino culture was extensive and lasting, beginning with the Catholic religion.

MENA2023_1.4_Ghost.name: North Anatolia Pontian Greeks
MENA2023_1.4_Ghost.overview: The Pontian Greeks got their name from an ancient kingdom on the southeastern coast of the Black Sea. They were originally colonists from ancient Greece. After the Ottoman Turks conquered this region in 1461, Pontian Greeks adopted Turkish language and culture, and many converted to Islam to have greater opportunities in Turkish society. In the face of assimilation, persecution, genocide, and forced emigration, they fought to preserve their distinct culture and language, which combined ancient Greek, Persian, and Turkish elements.

ASIA2023_4.3_Ghost.name: Khatri & Arora Punjabis
ASIA2023_4.3_Ghost.overview: The Khatris and Aroras are closely related ethnic groups from Sindh and Punjab. They are mostly Hindu but with connections to Sikhism. With a background in textile production, these small groups found outsized success in Punjabi, and then British, imperial administration. In the Sikh Empire, many Khatris and Aroras worked as munshis, or scribes; others built fortunes and imposing havelis (small palaces) from trading cloth, spices, and other goods. After India’s independence, many Khatris and Aroras used their business networks to build success in its economy or migrated to find new opportunities elsewhere.

MENA2023_2.2.3.name: Iraq
MENA2023_2.2.3.overview: Iraq’s rich history encompasses the territory of ancient Mesopotamia, located between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. It is known as the “cradle of civilization” because people of the region developed some of the world’s earliest writing, literature, sciences, mathematics, laws, and religions. Over the centuries, the inhabitants were influenced by many civilizations and empires. Iraq has always been an ethnically diverse country, with Arabs, Kurds, Assyrians, and Turkmen representing the largest ethnic groups. Many religions, including Islam, Christianity, Judaism, and Mandaeism, have adherents there.

ASIA2023_1.1.1.4_1.1.1.3_Ghost.name: Japan
ASIA2023_1.1.1.4_1.1.1.3_Ghost.overview: In the last two hundred years, the Japanese people have experienced their share of tragedies, from the Great Tenpo Famine of the 19th century to the devastation inflicted by bombing during World War II. But they also thrived during periods of excitement, creativity, and community strength: villagers banding together in the face of samurai abuse, intellectuals debating modernity over coffee, enterprising chefs combining Western techniques and local ingredients to make iconic new dishes, and employees, businesses, and government uniting to create Japan’s “economic miracle.”

MENA2023_2.1.5.name: Central Asia—South
MENA2023_2.1.5.overview: The mountainous region centered around the modern countries of Afghanistan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan is often described as Turko-Persia, a reference to the historical, cultural, and political traditions of the peoples of these lands. The label, of course, cannot capture the complete diversity of this region in which Pashtuns, Tajiks, Uzbeks, Turkmen, Hazaras, Aimaqs, and Kirgiz, to name just a few, often live side by side in the growing cities of Kabul and Tashkent. Most of the people of this region, however, still maintain the rural lifestyle of their ancestors as herders and subsistence farmers in the deserts, steppes, and mountains of these lands in the heart of Asia.

ASIA2023_2.1.5.name: Bicol
ASIA2023_2.1.5.overview: The Bicol region of the Philippines occupies the southeastern peninsula of Luzon Island plus several adjacent islands. Bicolano dialects, Tagalog, Spanish, and English languages evidence the region’s range of influences from indigenous traditions, Spanish and American colonial history, and maritime interactions. Across time, the region’s volcanic geography and storm-prone climate have yielded both beauty and peril, bounty and loss. Communities have survived and thrived through fishing and cultivating coconut, rice, and Manila hemp (abacá). Despite setbacks, Bicolano culture has embodied the belief that where there is life, there is hope.

ASIA2023_2.2.1_2.2.2_2.2.3_Ghost.name: Northern & Central Luzon & Central Calabarzon

subjourneys.ASIA2023_2.2.2: Central & Southern Ilocos, Northern Zambales & Tarlac

ASIA2023_2.2.1_2.2.2_2.2.3_Ghost.overview: Residents of the Ilocos region and the Lingayen Gulf enjoyed lucrative trade with the lowlands. Tobacco, rice, and sugar drew aspiring farmers and created many so-called “old Filipino elites.” Soon, the area was home to some of the fastest-growing towns outside Manila. Northern and central Luzon also became sources of revolutionaries who fought the Americans and formed the largest peasant association and the first communist guerilla army. After the devastation of World War II, many left to find work rebuilding Manila.

MENA2023_1.8.name: Southern & Eastern European Roma
MENA2023_1.8.overview: The Romani, also called Roma, came to Europe from northern India in the Middle Ages. In English they were called “Gypsies” because many Europeans once believed that they came from Egypt. The Romani have been one of the most persecuted minorities in Europe for centuries, which forced them to become nomadic. Today, most Romani are permanently settled and make up the largest ethnic minority in Europe. The largest concentrations of Romani live in central and southeastern Europe, and the Romani language, řomanes, includes more than 80 dialects.

ASIA2023_4.4.name: Central Asia—North
ASIA2023_4.4.overview: The people of Central Asia—including Turkic and Iranian populations, among others—have historically been rural and semi-nomadic, but the Silk Road trade routes from 200 BC to the 18th century also included several important cities. Their rich cultural heritage includes Uzbek literature, Kazakh oral histories, and Turkic cuisine. In the 1800s, the Russian Empire occupied most of this region and after 1918 it became part of the Soviet Union. Although the Soviet Union promoted some forms of artistic expression, censorship and repression were the norm for decades. However, the arts, literature, and other cultural activities slowly reemerged in the later 20th century.

MENA2023_1.6.name: Eastern Armenia & Iran
MENA2023_1.6.overview: Armenians have played a significant role in the Middle East, the Caucasus, and Iran for millennia. They have lived at the crossroads of powerful empires for thousands of years. Divided between rival states, the Armenian people experienced two different historical trajectories. Western Armenians, facing forced deportation or near extermination, sought refuge in migration to the Middle East, Europe, and the United States. Eastern Armenians remained in the Caucasus and Iran and ultimately gained independence for the Republic of Armenia in 1991.

MENA2023_1.7.name: Georgia
MENA2023_1.7.overview: Located in the Southern Caucasus region, at what is often referred to as a “crossroads” between Europe and Asia, Georgia is a small country with a rich history and a diverse natural and cultural landscape. While the entire country is roughly the size of North Carolina, Georgia boasts impressive ecological diversity and several distinct climate zones, from subtropical to high alpine to semidesert (in the east).  Despite a turbulent history marked by repeated conquest, Georgia’s unique language and alphabet, ancient winemaking traditions, and polyphonic music practices have survived to present day.

ASIA2023_1.4.8.name: Vietnam
ASIA2023_1.4.8.overview: Although deeply influenced by their imposing Chinese neighbor, the Vietnamese are one of Asia’s oldest civilizations. Veneration for ancestors and respect for community and family customs are long-held values. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, French colonialism’s emphasis on commercial agriculture disrupted traditional village life. Peasants moved from their rice paddies and fishing waters into increasingly crowded cities. A civil war between 1954 and 1975 caused immense death and devastation. But despite a difficult history, Vietnamese culture has adapted and survived.

ASIA2023_2.4.name: Western Visayas
ASIA2023_2.4.overview: Maritime life, culture, and industry were central to the Western Visayas. On Panay, textile weaving and eventually sugar were economic mainstays for the lowland town of Iloilo. As sugar plantations took hold, traffic increased between the islands of Panay, Negros, and Cebu, and plantation owners, workers, and peasant farmers saw new innovations in entertainment, literature, and modernization. The 20th century brought a surge of labor unions and protests that, after World War II, tried to protect those impacted by the damage to the region’s once booming economy.

ASIA2023_4.2.name: North Indian Muslims
ASIA2023_4.2.overview: North Indian Muslims descended from Afghan, Persian, and Turkic ancestors as well as local people who converted to Islam. They wove Islamic traditions and regional influences from the Indo-Gangetic plain into a rich Indo-Islamic culture. While sharing culture and language with their Hindu counterparts, North Indian Muslims had to deal with complex questions about whether they should live in a country of their own or a shared one with Indians of other religions.

ASIA2023_1.5.name: Korea
ASIA2023_1.5.overview: Between 1850 and 1975, the southern half of the Korean Peninsula dramatically changed from being an insular, agrarian society to an emerging industrialized economy. Seoul, the capital, grew in population and wealth. Clothing, diet, and housing became more Westernized, and a new middle class emerged. Social status became tied less to family connection and more to individual merit, especially in terms of education. As the country rebuilt after the Korean War, more Koreans turned to organized religion, gender roles changed, and a consumer culture emerged.

ASIA2023_Guangdong_Ghost.name: Guangdong
ASIA2023_Guangdong_Ghost.overview: For years, Guangdong and the Pearl River Delta were a vibrant center of trade—and the only Chinese port open to Western nations. Over time, economic hardship, natural disasters, and ineffective government led millions of Cantonese to immigrate. Many found their way to Chinatowns in the United States, where they transplanted Cantonese language and culture and waited for the chance to reunite with family. Others remained to weather war and the changes that came as the Communists took control and looked to build a new China.

ASIA2023_1.3.4.name: Bengal Delta
ASIA2023_1.3.4.overview: The residents of the Bengal Delta, an important trading region since the late 18th century, have faced profound ecological, social, and political changes. The region had long been among the world’s most fertile and prosperous, attracting migrants from other parts of India. But colonialism damaged the region’s economy, and the region became subject to environmental disaster, famine, and rural poverty. In 1947, the region was split politically between Hindu-dominated West Bengal, a state of modern India, and East Bengal, a part of Pakistan. Ultimately, East Bengal would become the new state of Bangladesh after a bloody war in 1971.

ASIA2023_1.6.1.name: Indentured Indian Diaspora
ASIA2023_1.6.1.overview: The large-scale influx of Indian migration to the Caribbean and Fiji began in the 19th century as contracted workers reshaped the cultural landscape of both regions. Workers from north India, committed to five-year contracts, endured harsh conditions on sugar plantations. Few returned to India as they initially hoped. Over time, distinct Indo-Caribbean and Fiji Hindi cultures emerged, mixing Indian traditions with local influences. After their contracts ended, many Indians sought new economic opportunities, from farming to shop-owning and dock work. By the mid-20th century, the majority had moved from agriculture to work in urban economies, forging distinct Indian communities far away from the Indian subcontinent.

ASIA2023_Indonesia_Ghost.name: Indonesia
ASIA2023_Indonesia_Ghost.overview: Spread across thousands of islands, modern Indonesia is home to hundreds of ethnic groups and languages. Its location in the ring of fire has also left it vulnerable to natural disasters, including the eruption of Krakatoa in the 19th century that obliterated many of the surrounding settlements. For centuries, Indonesians depended on subsistence agriculture and communal child-rearing. Dutch colonial rule, urbanization, and globalization changed Indonesians’ lives and lifestyles, but they have maintained the diverse culinary and cultural traditions the region is famous for today.

ASIA2023_1.3.2.3.name: Peninsular Malaysia
ASIA2023_1.3.2.3.overview: In the centuries leading up to independence, the people of Peninsular Malaysia lived through colonial rule, economic transformation, and profound social change. The states of Kedah, Penang, Malacca, and the growing capital of Kuala Lumpur were shaped by the ebb and flow of regional trade, immigration, European ambitions, and resilient local communities. Farmers, fishermen, traders, and laborers adapted to each new wave of rulers, while religious and cultural traditions—rooted in Malay, Chinese, Indian, and European influences—flourished.

MENA2023_4.1_4.3_Ghost.name: Southern Levant
MENA2023_4.1_4.3_Ghost.overview: The Levant includes areas comprised of the modern territories of Cyprus, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine, Syria, and Turkey. At the crossroads of Europe, Asia, and Africa, it has always been a hub where diverse peoples intermingled. Its strategic location and religious significance gave added importance. From 1516 to 1918, the region formed part of the Ottoman Empire, which governed the area through taxes, tariffs on trade, and oversight of the legal system. The diverse peoples of the Levant, unified by their strong communities and religious ties, were able to adapt to continuously changing circumstances.

MENA2023_2.2.2.name: Arabian Peninsula
MENA2023_2.2.2.overview: For most of its history, regional tribes controlled the Arabian Peninsula. In the early 1500s, the Ottoman Empire began to oversee the Hijaz region and pilgrimage routes to Mecca and Medina. But despite Ottoman influence and widespread adherence to Islam, Arab communities along the Red Sea maintained some distinct beliefs and cultural practices. Distinctions began to fade as the Al Saud dynasty and Wahhabi Islam gained prominence, uniting Arabia’s tribes into a kingdom. The early 20th century's discovery of oil brought wealth, modernization, and social complexities to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

LA2023_Azores_Ghost.overview: The Azores are a group of nine volcanic islands in the North Atlantic Ocean that were settled mostly by people from mainland Portugal. The islands played an important role in Portuguese exploration. By the early 1800s, many Azoreans began leaving the islands because of economic struggles, crowded living conditions, and limited farmland. Some went to California, where they used their farming and dairy skills, while others moved to Hawaii or the East Coast of the United States. In their new homes, Azoreans worked to keep their traditions alive by celebrating Holy Spirit festivals, cooking traditional foods, and decorating with volcanic rock and colorful religious tiles.

MENA2023_Cyprus_Ghost.name: Cyprus
MENA2023_Cyprus_Ghost.overview: Due to its location in the eastern Mediterranean Sea, the island of Cyprus has changed hands many times. In antiquity it experienced Assyrian, Egyptian, Persian, Greek, and Roman rule, interrupted by only brief periods of independence. During the modern period, social and political divisions between the island’s two main groups—Turkish Cypriots and Greek Cypriots—led to conflict and unrest that worsened under eight decades of British occupation. After Cyprus gained independence, tens of thousands escaped political and economic insecurity by emigrating.

MENA2023_2.2.6.name: Gulf of Aden
MENA2023_2.2.6.overview: Since the origins of the frankincense and myrrh trade in ancient times, Yemen and northern Somalia have supported sultans, sheikhs, nomads, and city dwellers. In contrast to the arid lowlands, the more hospitable highlands supported larger-scale farming and settled communities. People traded goods and shared culture over land and sea routes, connecting the Arabian Peninsula, the Horn of Africa, and other regions. Long before the influence of Saudi oil wealth began to affect the region, the religious and cultural practices of Sunni Islam and Sufism shaped the spiritual and social landscape.

ASIA2023_2.1.1.name: Fujian & Taiwan
ASIA2023_2.1.1.overview: Taiwan's mountainous spine, fertile coastal plains, and location along Pacific trade routes have supported people for millennia. The island's Indigenous peoples developed knowledge of mountain forests and marine resources over generations. Beginning in the Dutch period, Chinese settlers from Fujian and Guangdong Provinces introduced intensive rice cultivation and sugar production. The Japanese colonial period brought scientific forestry, modern medicine, and urban planning. After World War II, Taiwan's population swelled with the arrival of the KMT government and millions from mainland China. This spurred urbanization and industry but also created political and social tensions.

GreatBritain_NWEngland_Ghost.name: North West England & Northern Wales

GreatBritain_NWEngland_Ghost.overview: Farming, weaving, and even mining had long been family and cottage industries for people from Cheshire to Lancashire. But as the Industrial Revolution changed Britain’s place in the world, it changed the lives of the people in the country’s manufacturing and shipping centers. Overpopulated cities became vital hubs of industry, where mills and factories churned out goods for the world. They also became miserable homes for workers in the 19th century, who would organize and fight for a better life in the 20th.

EEU2023_Lithuania_Ghost.overview: A Baltic nation, Lithuania has a long and proud history. Over centuries, Lithuanians developed a strong national identity, based on their language, unique folk traditions, and strong Catholic faith. Even when powerful neighboring countries tried to take control, or during times of war and hardship, Lithuanians worked to keep their culture alive. Many also moved to other parts of the world, but they still held on to their traditions. This strong connection to their culture helped Lithuanian people preserve their identity, even during difficult times.

IRL2018_1.2.5_1.2.3.overview: Among the rolling hills and green pastures of the Irish lowlands, most inhabitants of central Ireland carved out a living on small plots of land. They lived in rural areas, spoke Irish, and practiced Catholicism. Ireland’s history is plagued by years of famine and centuries of clashes over religion, which led millions to seek a new life elsewhere. The most common destination was the United States, where Irish Americans’ political and cultural contributions created a distinct Irish-American identity and made them a vital part of American life.

DE_2021_1.1.3.1.name: Luxembourg

subjourneys.DE_2021_1.1.3.1.2.2: Luxembourg to Ettelbruck to German Border

DE_2021_1.1.3.1.overview: The people of Luxembourg have a distinct national identity, their own language (Lëtzebuergesch), a strong Roman Catholic tradition, and are a mix of French and German cultural influences. Throughout history, they were frequently invaded and ruled by their much larger and more powerful neighbors. During the 18th century, most Luxembourgers were primarily small-scale farmers and craftspeople, working as potters, tanners, or brewers. After the country gained independence in 1839, Luxembourgers experienced gradual industrialization into the 20th century, especially after World War II, and found increased prosperity.

IRL2018_1.2.10.overview: In the late 1700s the population of Ulster was growing. Land was scarce, rents were high, and many were persecuted for their religious beliefs. As poverty, famine, and unemployment continued throughout the 1800s, some Ulster Irish immigrated to America, England, and Scotland looking for a better life. Others remained in their homeland and braved world wars, internal political and religious division, civil war, and the birth of Northern Ireland.

DE_2021_1.1.2.3.overview: Bavaria and Bohemia were regions in the Holy Roman Empire whose shared southern border had been devastated during the Thirty Years’ War. The borderlands were not heavily populated or particularly fertile. Many people worked in cottage-based textiles, or they moved to areas more hospitable to farming. German was spoken in both regions, but most Bohemians were Czech speakers. Catholicism profoundly shaped most people’s lives. After centuries of struggle, thousands of Bavarians and Bohemians emigrated to the Upper Midwest of the United States, settling mostly in Wisconsin. Over a few generations, they largely integrated into mainstream American culture.

LA2023_CanaryIslands_Ghost.name: Canary Islands
LA2023_CanaryIslands_Ghost.overview: The Canary Islands lie off the coast of northwest Africa. Spanish colonizers arrived in the 1400s, and over the next century, war, disease, and assimilation brought an end to the native Guanches culture and people. The islands became an important stop on Atlantic trade routes, and by the 1700s, a stream of Canarians had migrated to Cuba and Puerto Rico, eager to work in the growing tobacco and sugar trades. Over time, Canary Islanders crafted a unique identity, culture, and dialect that influenced countries throughout the Caribbean.

EEU2023_PodlachiaWarmiaMasuria_Ghost.name: North Central Poland
EEU2023_PodlachiaWarmiaMasuria_Ghost.overview: The fertile lands of northeastern Poland have supported farming and raising animals for centuries. With deep roots in Roman Catholicism, Poles built pilgrimage sites and churches across the region. Starting in the 19th century, and continuing over decades, many Poles left the region because of political upheaval, war, economic hardship, and communist repression. Today, some 20 million people of Polish heritage live outside of Poland, in a variety of countries, but especially in cities like Chicago and across the U.S. Northeast.

EEU2023_CzechMoravia_Ghost.overview: The region of Moravia encompasses almost the entire eastern side of today’s Czech Republic. Some of the country’s largest cities are in this region, which is covered in green foothills and an intricate river system. For centuries, Moravia had been an economic powerhouse, particularly after the discovery of important mineral resources in the 19th century, bringing prosperity to the Habsburg Empire and later to Czechoslovakia. Ethnically speaking, Czechs predominated, but there were also significant populations of Germans, Jews, and Poles.

IRL2018_1.1.3_1.1.2.name: Connacht, Ireland

subjourneys.IRL2018_1.1.3.7.1: West Roscommon, East Mayo & North Galway

IRL2018_1.1.3_1.1.2.overview: Life was difficult for the people of Connacht at the turn of the 19th century. As the population grew, land became scarce, and families who couldn't afford their rent were often evicted from their homes with little notice. During the Great Famine, many in the west died or fled to escape poverty and starvation. Many traveled to America's East Coast, settling in cities like New York and Boston. Others landed in England or Australia. Life was slow to change in Connacht, and the region is still home to the highest percentage of Irish speakers in Ireland.

MENA2019_1.4.1.name: South Greece
MENA2019_1.4.1.overview: The region of southern Greece consists primarily of the Peloponnese. Peloponnesian Greeks were nurtured in a land rich with history, myth, and culture, from the most ancient Greeks to their modern descendants who preserve their own distinctive cultures, cuisine, and art. Greek drama was born in Epidaurus, and the Olympic Games in Olympia. The people and customs of this region were further enriched by Venetian and Slavic cultures. As the population grew in this resource-poor land, many Greeks migrated, carrying their customs and culture to the wider world.

EEU2023_Belarus_Ghost.name: Eastern Lithuania & Western Belarus
EEU2023_Belarus_Ghost.overview: A land of rolling landscapes marked by dense forests, glacial lakes, and gentle hills, the historic Vilnius (Vilna) region was a remarkable mosaic of cultural diversity. From the 1700s onward, the area was home to a complex linguistic and ethnic landscape: Polish-speaking nobles and gentry coexisted with Lithuanian peasants, Belarusian farmers, and significant Jewish communities. Yiddish, Polish, Lithuanian, and Belarusian languages intermingled. The region's cold winters and mild summers shaped agricultural practices and community life, supporting a predominantly rural population that maintained unique cultural traditions across generations.

DE_2021_1.1.1.1.4.2.name: German Palatines in Lower Austria, Central Poland & Western Ukraine
DE_2021_1.1.1.1.4.2.overview: A collection of feudal territories in the Rhine River valley, the Rhineland-Palatinate (in present-day southwestern Germany) was, for part of its history, a buffer region between warring powers. Those powers frequently tested the strength of the region’s fortifications and destroyed its fields and vineyards. Peasants fled by the thousands, securing opportunities in other lands, including Lower Austria and Austrian Galicia. There they lived quiet lives in agriculture for most of the 19th century, until political changes severely restricted their opportunities. Near the beginning of the 20th century, thousands were uprooted again, this time bound for the prairies of Canada.

SCAND2018_4.2.name: Iceland
SCAND2018_4.2.overview: After seafaring Norse settlers migrated to Iceland in the 9th century, they struggled against diseases, volcanic eruptions, and a poor climate while eking out their existence. Farms dotted the little arable land, producing enough hay to feed the livestock that provided milk and cheese. Fishermen ventured out in winter and spring to catch herring and cod. In the 19th century, with a growing population and little available land, many young Icelanders had little choice but to leave. They formed successful and close-knit communities in places like Canada and Minnesota.

GreatBritain_2021_2.5.name: North England & Scotland Border

subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_2.5.4: Central & Eastern Northumberland to Eastern Durham

GreatBritain_2021_2.5.overview: England was the epicenter of the Industrial Revolution, and northern England was at its core. What was once a collection of agricultural lands and market towns was transformed into densely populated cities, complete with factories and paved roads. Urban growing pains, overcrowding, disease, and inequality gave some English families no choice but to leave. Many took advantage of Britain’s vast global empire, making the long voyage to then-colonies Australia and New Zealand, while later populations stayed closer to home, moving to the Midlands and London.

SCAND2018_1.1.name: Central & Southern Sweden
SCAND2018_1.1.overview: Southwest Sweden, consisting of the counties of Västra Götaland, Halland, and part of Småland is historically one of Sweden’s most populous and productive regions. Gothenburg—one of Sweden’s most important trading and shipping centers—lies on the west coast. Throughout the 1700s and 1800s, the region provided the rest of Sweden with cattle, household goods, and tools. In the mid-1800s, traditional Swedish life built on agriculture and local trade began to disintegrate as millions of Swedes sought work in urban areas and in America.

MENA2019_1.4.2.1.name: Albania, Northern Greece & North Macedonia
MENA2019_1.4.2.1.overview: Southeastern Albania, northern Greece, and southwestern North Macedonia are covered by rugged mountains and thick forests. This area has always been one of the most ethnically and linguistically diverse parts of Europe. The Ottoman Empire’s invasions from the 14th<sup> </sup>to the 18th centuries converted some of Europe’s oldest Christians to Islam. Recurrent warfare and political strife in the modern period not only threatened this diversity, but caused many Albanians, Greeks, Turks, Macedonians, Bulgarians, and various other Slavic peoples to emigrate.

DE_2021_7.3.name: Protestant Black Sea Germans

subjourneys.DE_2021_7.3.3: Black Sea Germans—Glückstal, Neudorf, Kassel, Bergdorf
subjourneys.DE_2021_7.3.2: Black Sea Germans—Beresan and Liebental enclaves

DE_2021_7.3.overview: Protestant Germans living in the Holy Roman Empire endured generations of wars, high taxes, scarcity of land, and religious intolerance after the Reformation. Napoleon brought more unrest to the region, driving some Germans from their homes in the southern German states and Alsace. So when the chance came to move to South Russia where there was plenty of land and promises of freedom, thousands of families settled in provinces along the Black Sea near Odesa, Ukraine today. Life changed again as their freedoms were revoked. Some stayed in Russia and experienced more unrest and war, but many moved again to start a new life in North America.

MENA2019_1.4.2.3.name: Western Balkans
MENA2019_1.4.2.3.overview: The Western Balkans comprises seven modern-day countries: Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, Albania, Serbia, Kosovo, and North Macedonia. Throughout history, this region has been carved up by foreign empires, each leaving a distinct mark. As a result, the Western Balkans has long been a melting pot of cultural, religious, and linguistic diversity, commonly said to be where “east” meets “west.” With the exception of Albania, all of these countries were once united under one political entity, Yugoslavia, first from 1918-1941 and then again from 1945-1991.

GreatBritain_2021_1.4.1.name: Devon, Dorset & Somerset

subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_1.4.1.3: Central Eastern Devon to Eastern Cornwall

GreatBritain_2021_1.4.1.overview: By the 1700s, residents of Devon, Dorset, and Somerset were often small-scale farmers, fishers, and skilled craftsmen. The mild climate of the region allowed the people to grow a variety of crops and breed and care for domestic animals. Copper, coal, and tin mining helped to solidify the reputation of South West England’s skilled laborers, providing them with opportunities to work abroad in Australia and New Zealand. People in the region also played a critical role during conflicts of the 20th century by providing shelter to war refugees and offering land to be used for military training.

SCAND2018_1.2.name: Northern Sweden
SCAND2018_1.2.overview: Sweden’s northern provinces, collectively referred to as Norrland, comprise the most sparsely populated region of the country. In the 1700s and 1800s locals mined iron and copper, raised livestock and reindeer, and harvested fish and seals along the coast. Until the 20th century, the rugged and cold environment led to frequent crop failures and famines. Because life was so difficult, many northern Swedes emigrated in the 1800s, first to cities in Sweden and later to America, where they became wheat farmers, loggers, miners, domestic servants, and craftsmen.

DE_2021_7.4_1.1.1.5_Ghost.overview: In the 1700s, most Germanic Europeans were serfs with limited rights and property. German kingdoms had been divided into Catholic and Protestant denominations by the Reformation. Many of these Germans moved to the Russian steppes to escape war and religious persecution. They settled along the Volga River in small, self-sufficient communities called colonies. Over the following century, Volga Germans found prosperity, usually farming and milling wheat, but the threat of mandatory military service drove them to North America, where they joined their German American counterparts in the Great Plains.
