GreatBritain_2021_3.3.1_3.3.2_3.3.3_Ghos.overview: The Industrial Revolution changed how people lived and what they did for a living in the Midlands. It changed how land was farmed, what was manufactured, and who was doing the work. Towns and cities such as Birmingham, Stoke-on-Trent, Nottingham, and Leicester became centers of production, drawing employees from the land to work in new industries. Wages were usually higher in the cities, though working conditions were often tough. Despite this, many areas remained rural, and life there changed comparatively little.

MENA2019_1.4.3.name: West Anatolia & Aegean Islands
MENA2019_1.4.3.overview: This community includes the Aegean islands and Crete, as well as the eastern coast of Greece and the western coast of Asia Minor. The islands are among the best-known features of Greece. Populated from ancient times by colonists from mainland Greece, the islands have contributed to the maritime culture, intellectual ferment, and industry of Greece throughout history. The Minoan civilization on Crete was the oldest known in the region. Philosophy, science, and medicine were born in the coastal cities on the eastern side of the Aegean Sea.

DE_2021_Rhineland_Ghost.name: The Rhineland
DE_2021_Rhineland_Ghost.overview: The Rhineland is an area of western Germany along the banks of the Rhine River. The Rhine River has long served as a key transportation route, as well as a source of fish and gold deposits. Grapevines for winemaking have been grown along its banks since Roman times. Until the middle of the 19th century, most inhabitants were farmers. In the latter half of the century, the Rhineland became an industrial hub.

SEUR2019_2.6.name: Northern Sicily
SEUR2019_2.6.overview: Because of Sicily’s strategic and agricultural importance, several empires have ruled it over the past millennia. As a result, Sicilians have an incredibly diverse history and language, influenced by ancient Greek, Roman, Arabic, Byzantine, Norman, and Spanish peoples. Palermo has long been the capital and cultural center of the island, as well as its largest city. Sicilians live in a geologically active zone, and their lives have often been disrupted by earthquakes and eruptions of Mt. Etna in the east, the largest active volcano in Europe.

IRL2018_1.3.name: Munster, Ireland

subjourneys.IRL2021_NM_2.16: North East Limerick & North West Tipperary
subjourneys.IRL2021_NM_top.2: North East Munster & South West Leinster

IRL2018_1.3.overview: Cradled by mountains and covered by a patchwork of inhospitable bogs, Munster was the perfect hiding place for rebels and outlaws who sought refuge from British authority. During the Great Famine, many Munster inhabitants fled their homes to escape poverty and starvation. With one of the highest and most consistent emigration levels in Europe, hundreds of thousands left the shores of Ireland for Victoria in southeastern Australia or the United States, where they settled in New York, Boston, or other urban centers across the American Midwest.

GreatBritain_2021_2.1.4.name: Southwestern Scotland & Northern Ulster
GreatBritain_2021_2.1.4.overview: The history of South West Scotland is intimately connected with its nearest neighbor, the North of Ireland. Just twelve miles apart at their nearest point, the close connection of the two areas is reflected not only in their shared history but also in the DNA of the descendants of those who lived there. Over the centuries, there have been migrations in both directions with people seeking new opportunities or escaping famine, hardship, and religious persecution. Some eventually sought new lives overseas where their hard work helped to build the new communities where they settled.

DE_2021_1.2.4.1.name: Northeastern Germany
DE_2021_1.2.4.1.overview: On the coast of the Baltic Sea, the rolling hills and fertile soil of northeastern Germany sustained farmers for centuries. A series of wars and military occupations made life difficult for those in this largely rural region, but most people benefited from close-knit communities that helped one another during times of conflict, famine, or disease. Industrialization brought unprecedented challenges to the area, and many people left their villages for larger cities or emigrated. Northeastern Germans also experienced changes following World War II, when partitioned Germany became the epicenter of the Cold War and the standoff between East and West.

DE_2021_1.2.4.2.name: Schleswig-Holstein
DE_2021_1.2.4.2.overview: Located on the southern portion of the Jutland peninsula, Schleswig-Holstein includes coastal marshlands, sandy plains, and fertile clay soils. Starting in the 1700s, small farms and large estates developed to create flax and dairy products for market. Residents of the area have historically identified with either or both Danish and German culture, resulting in numerous upheavals. These conflicts, along with slow modernization, led many to emigrate and settle in the American Midwest from the 1840s onward, where they created tight-knit communities.

LA2023_Portugual_Ghost.name: Portugal

subjourneys.LA2023_1.1.8: Porto | São João da Madeira | Aveiro

LA2023_Portugual_Ghost.overview: The Portuguese have a long history as a seafaring people who built a global empire through colonization in Latin America, Asia, and Africa. Along Portugal’s rugged coastline, many worked as fishermen, whalers, sailors, and traders, while most inland inhabitants focused on agriculture. Predominantly Catholic, many Portuguese value family time and celebrating traditional holidays. The nation is known for its ornate architecture and distinctive azulejos—vibrant, hand-painted ceramic tiles that adorn buildings and public spaces. Portuguese heritage also shines through in soulful fado music, rich folklore, and a culinary tradition featuring hearty soups, the iconic dried and salted cod known as bacalhau, and world-renowned wines.

SEUR2019_2.5.name: Central Eastern Italy
SEUR2019_2.5.overview: Inhabited since the Stone Age, Naples and surrounding southern Italy has long been an important cultural, political, and agricultural region. The warm Mediterranean climate attracted foreign merchants and travelers who marveled at the region’s natural beauty and its inhabitants’ way of life. By the late 19th century, however, the cities could no longer support the growing population, with rural peasants living in poverty due to recurrent crop failures and agrarian crises. In the following decades, millions of Italians crossed the Atlantic to start anew in the United States, where they forged a distinctive identity.

SCAND2018_6.4.name: Central & Southern Finland

subjourneys.SCAND2018_6.4.3.1: Lapland, Finland, Northern Sweden & Northern Norway
subjourneys.SCAND2018_6.4.3: North Finland & the Sami Lands of Norway & Sweden

SCAND2018_6.4.overview: Life in central and eastern Finland differed from life in the western and southern parts of the country. The population was sparser, and residents contended with a harsher landscape as they made their living from the forests and lakes. Russia also had a stronger influence on the culture. The 19th century brought both severe famines and new jobs in Finland’s developing forest economy. It also saw population growth and dissatisfaction with Russian rule spur thousands of eastern Finns to emigrate to the United States and Canada.

EEU2023_Slovakia_Ghost.name: Slovakia

subjourneys.EEU2023_2.3.4.1: East Central Prešov & East Central Košice
subjourneys.EEU2023_2.3.1.3: Eastern Prešov, Eastern Košice & Hungary Border
subjourneys.EEU2023_2.3.1.2.1: South Central Prešov & North Central Košice
subjourneys.EEU2023_2.2.3: Sabinov, Stará Ľubovňa, Bardejov & Poland Border
subjourneys.EEU2023_5.3.1.4: South Central Žilina & North Central Banská Bystrica

EEU2023_Slovakia_Ghost.overview: Over the centuries, the Slovak people lived through imperial rule, various wars and revolutions, and much economic hardship. Those who stayed in Europe dealt with political, economic, and cultural sea changes, while those who emigrated to North America struggled to make ends meet with jobs in industry and farming. By the early 20th century, Slovakian immigrants thrived in tight-knit ethnic communities from New York to Chicago by establishing mutual aid societies and Slovak Catholic churches to support one another through the upheaval that defined the modern era. In both Europe and North America, they maintained their distinct sense of identity.

SEUR2019_1.5.2.name: Western Croatia
SEUR2019_1.5.2.overview: Just as the Adriatic Sea is central to modern Croatian identity, the Kvarner Bay area is central to the history of the Istrian region. There, the early population of ethnic Italians and ethnic Croats was later enlarged by German and Hungarian groups. Istria was long part of the Habsburg Empire, which developed Rijeka into a major port city. As in the rest of Croatia, many residents worked in shipping, but this area also had strong ties to the inland mountains.

SEUR2019_1.5.3.name: Croatia
SEUR2019_1.5.3.overview: Croatia’s central Dalmatia includes historically significant port cities along the Adriatic Sea such as Split and Hvar. It also takes in some of the country’s largest islands and peninsulas, including Korčula, Brač, and Pelješac. Coastal areas retain a Mediterranean influence from many years as part of the Venetian Empire. Inland areas, known as the “Dalmatian Hinterland,” have their own cultures similar to rural peasant populations throughout central and southern Europe. Reliance on the land—whether for viticulture or grain farming—and religious faith shape daily life and culture.

EEU2023_HungaryEast_Ghost.name: Eastern Hungary
EEU2023_HungaryEast_Ghost.overview: The inhabitants of Eastern Hungary were a diverse group of Hungarian, Slovak, and German speakers who reflected a wide range of cultural traditions and ethnic backgrounds. These communities endured many economic and social upheavals during the 18th, 19th, and 20th centuries, but poverty and the promise of economic opportunity prompted many to emigrate. The strong cultural bonds of these Eastern Hungarian immigrants continued to exert broad influence on the communities that were established in North America in places like Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan, and Illinois.

EEU2023_Latvia_Ghost.name: Latvia
EEU2023_Latvia_Ghost.overview: Latvia, alongside Lithuania and Estonia, belongs to the Baltic region in Europe. With a mixed population of ethnic Latvians and Russians, the sparsely populated country enjoys a temperate climate and thick spruce, birch, and pine forests. Known as “Livonia” or “Lettland” until the 19th century, Latvia was ruled by the Russian Empire for several centuries before enjoying a brief period of independence between the First and Second World Wars. In the late 19th century and throughout the 20th century, many Latvians left their homeland for North America or Australia in search of economic opportunity and freedom from war and political oppression.

SCAND2018_3.4.name: Southeastern, Central & Northern Norway

subjourneys.SCAND2018_3.4.1.4.3: Nordre Land, Søndre Land & Northern Toten & Ringsakker
subjourneys.SCAND2018_3.4.4.3: Northern Hedmark, Southeastern Trøndelag & Northeastern Dalarnas län
subjourneys.SCAND2018_3.4.3.2: Northern Møre og Romsdal, Oppland & Northern Hedmark
subjourneys.SCAND2018_3.4.1: Southern Hedmark, Eastern Akershus & Southern Oppland

SCAND2018_3.4.overview: For centuries, the people of northern and eastern Norway have farmed; hunted reindeer; fished and traded herring, cod, salmon, and furs; and mined iron and copper in the mountains near the Swedish border. In the 18th century, life was marked by the seasonal harvest and fish catches, but also by increasing wealth brought by trade. In the 19th century, rapid population growth caused thousands from the Gudbrandsdalen and Lillehammer areas to leave for land and better lives in America, where they created communities that reminded them of home.

MENA2019_1.4.2.2.1.name: Bulgaria
MENA2019_1.4.2.2.1.overview: More than 13 centuries ago, Bulgaria was established on a vital international crossroads. Geography and the rise and fall of empires has shaped the Bulgarian people ever since. Living at Europe’s gateway to the East brought the benefits of varied cultural influences and trade, as well as drawbacks that came with conquest. Bulgarians often found themselves entangled in international conflicts without much say in them. Through it all, the long tradition of Christian faith helped many preserve their spirit and sense of national identity.

EEU2023_Austria_Ghost.name: Austria

subjourneys.EEU2023_1.1.5: Neusiedl am See & Eastern Eisenstadt-Umgebung Districts

EEU2023_Austria_Ghost.overview: The area that is present-day Austria has long been an intersection of German, Hungarian, and Croatian languages and cultures. Toward the end of the 19th century, many rural residents of this region immigrated to the U.S. and settled in cities like Saint Paul, New York, Chicago, and Trenton. They found employment in industries such as steel production, meatpacking, and masonry. Despite the prejudice they faced during both World Wars, these communities proved resilient, and their cultural traditions have endured for centuries.

DE_2021_RomaniaGermans_Ghost.name: Germans in Romania

subjourneys.DE_2021_1.1.3.2.2.1: Central Timis, Romania to Zrenjanin, Serbia
subjourneys.DE_2021_1.1.3.2.2.5: Cărpiniș to Comloșu Mare, Romania to Kikinda, Serbia

DE_2021_RomaniaGermans_Ghost.overview: From feudal territories in the Rhineland-Palatinate (a region in southwestern Germany) and the southern border with France, German speakers of the 18th century immigrated to Habsburg colonies in and around present-day Romania. Enjoying opportunities to own land, practice their Protestant religion, and send their children to state-sponsored schools, German communities thrived for about a century. But increasing nationalist sentiment and decreasing availability of land later made life difficult for the German-speaking minority. Many set their sights on the New World, where they integrated first into immigrant German communities and later into mainstream America.

DE_2021_7.2_7.5_Ghost.name: German Anabaptists

subjourneys.DE_2021_7.2: Chortitza & Molotschna Mennonites—Neuendorf, Chortitza, Halbstadt, Blumenort
subjourneys.DE_2021_7.5: Hutterites from Wischenka, Radichev, Hutterthal, Hutterdorf & Johannesruh
subjourneys.DE_2021_7.2.1: Chortitza & Molotschna Mennonites—Neuendorf, Schönhorst, Fürstenau, Schönsee

DE_2021_7.2_7.5_Ghost.overview: Dissatisfied with the reforms of the Protestant Reformation, Anabaptists, including the Amish, Hutterites, and Mennonites, wanted to return to principles of earlier Christianity. Among their beliefs were the separation of church and state, pacifism, and a strong emphasis on community. At odds with Catholic and Protestant authorities in Europe, these groups faced a long history of persecution and emigration. Hutterites and Mennonites immigrated to the Russian Empire where they were promised fertile land, freedom from military conscription, and freedom to practice their religion. When these rights were revoked, they moved to North America.

LA2023_Basque_Ghost.name: Basque Country
LA2023_Basque_Ghost.overview: The Basque Country stretches across the Pyrenees Mountains in both Spain and France. For centuries, Basques have kept a unique identity, separate from the European powers around them. Their language, Euskara, was sometimes banned by both Spain and France. Catholic traditions and farming played a big role in daily life, strengthening families and communities. In the early 1900s, changes brought by industry, political unrest, and financial hardship led many Basques to move to the United States. There, they kept their culture alive by creating boardinghouses, festivals, and social clubs that blended old traditions with new American experiences.

GreatBritain_2021_1.1.1_1.1.3_Ghost.name: East of England

subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_1.1.1: Central & East of England to London
subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_1.1.1.3: Central & Southern Cambridgeshire, Eastern Suffolk & Northwestern Essex

GreatBritain_2021_1.1.1_1.1.3_Ghost.overview: Living in England’s so-called “breadbasket,” East England’s residents have long been linked with the fortunes of farming. The Industrial Revolution, which vastly changed the need for laborers, was the main impetus behind many from Norfolk, Suffolk, and Essex moving from countryside to town, from town to industrialized cities, and even beyond England’s shores. These people embraced change, made improvements after disaster, and found opportunities even in war. They’ve also long been associated with non-conformism, and many became early immigrants to North America, Australia, and New Zealand.

GreatBritain_2021_1.2.2_1.2.3_1.2.4_Ghos.name: Eastern South East England

subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_1.2.2.1: West Sussex, West Surrey & Eastern East Surrey & Kent
subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_1.2.3: Central & Eastern East Sussex & Southern Kent

GreatBritain_2021_1.2.2_1.2.3_1.2.4_Ghos.overview: The counties of South East England have long served as a conduit between London and the European continent. Historically, the region’s people have devoted themselves to agriculture, fishing, trade, and service industries. The effects of the agricultural and Industrial revolutions came on slowly, but over time they pushed thousands out of the countryside and into London or faraway Australia or America. Although they suffered heavy losses during the world wars, Southeasterners showed resilience in remaking themselves, whether at home or abroad.

EJ2019_3.2.name: Ashkenazi Jews in Northeastern Europe

subjourneys.EJ2019_3.2.1.1: Ashkenazi Jews in Southwest Latvia & Lithuania
subjourneys.EJ2019_3.2.1: Ashkenazi Jews in Southwest Latvia, Lithuania & Northwest Belarus
subjourneys.EJ2019_3.2.2.1: Ashkenazi Jews in Belarus & Northern Ukraine

EJ2019_3.2.overview: The Ashkenazi Jews of Northern and Eastern Europe historically worked as traders, peddlers, grocers, and administrators of property owned by nobility. Many lived in small towns (shtetls) and spoke Yiddish. Set apart from Christian society by language and religion, they faced varying degrees of restriction and persecution. Although some European Jews tried integrating into Christian society, it made no difference in the end since Nazi Germany targeted all Jews, killing millions in the Holocaust. Hundreds of thousands of others were able to escape to the United States and elsewhere.

GreatBritain_2021_2.4.1_2.4.2_Ghost.name: East & Central Scottish Lowlands
GreatBritain_2021_2.4.1_2.4.2_Ghost.overview: The people of Eastern Scotland come from a region rich in history, language, and culture. The area encompasses the close-knit fishing villages of the east coast, the Doric-speaking rural communities of Aberdeenshire and the Mearns, as well as the Gaelic culture of the Central Highlands. Throughout the centuries, these hardy and hard-working people have traveled the world as seafarers, traders, soldiers, and explorers, seeking fortune and new lives overseas.

LA2023_SpainWestNorth_Ghost.name: Northern Spain

subjourneys.LA2023_2.2.4: Galicia, Asturias & Northwestern Castilla y Leon
subjourneys.LA2023_2.2.2: Eastern Galicia, Northern Castilla y Leon & Cantabria

LA2023_SpainWestNorth_Ghost.overview: Northern Spain is a region of diverse peoples, languages, and cultures. Bordering the Bay of Biscay and the Pyrenees Mountains, the Basques have long defended their way of life against outside rule. To the west lie Calabria, with its ancient port cities, and Asturias, with its rugged mountains. And, in the rainy coastal hills of Galicia, most people farmed or raised cattle. Over time, many people from northern Spain have immigrated to the United States, Argentina, and other destinations to escape political persecution and pursue new economic opportunities.

EEU2023_HungaryWest_Ghost.name: Western Hungary

subjourneys.EEU2023_7.3.3: Zala & Southern Vas Counties & Austria & Slovakia Borders

EEU2023_HungaryWest_Ghost.overview: The region that is now Western Hungary has for centuries been a meeting point for Hungarian, German, Jewish, and South Slavic cultures and languages. The people persevered through wars, epidemics, imperial rule, and poverty. In the early decades of the 20th century, many rural Hungarians emigrated to North America, in particular to the industrial cities of eastern Pennsylvania, and to Detroit and Toronto, leaving behind agricultural work for steady employment in factories and steel mills. They maintained their cultural communities through shared faith, food, and language while navigating prejudice in their ancestral and adopted homelands.

SEUR2019_2.3.name: Central Southwest Italy
SEUR2019_2.3.overview: The city of Naples, in the southern Italian region of Campania, gets its name from the Greek word Neapolis (Νεάπολις), meaning “New Town.” A cultural hub since the Roman Empire, it’s famed not only because it’s one of the oldest continuously inhabited urban areas in the world but also because of its volcanic activity. Mount Vesuvius is only six miles from the city center. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, overcrowding and poverty spurred la grande migrazione, an enormous immigration from Italy to the United States, where Italian Americans forged a new life and made a permanent impact on American culture.

SEUR2019_1.5.5.name: Northeast Italy
SEUR2019_1.5.5.overview: Like the rest of Italy, the northeast corner of the country was part of ancient Rome. In the early Middle Ages, it became the center of the Republic of Venice, a powerful and far-reaching maritime republic that lasted for more than a millennium before falling to French and Austrian rule and finally joining a unified Italy in 1866. The people of Northeast Italy lived at a cultural crossroads, often speaking German rather than Italian, and were known for Germanic delicacies like apple strudel as much as for tiramisu. Because of the struggles that followed unification, many Italians immigrated to North America.

EEU2023_PolandPomerania_Ghost.name: Gdansk Pomerania

subjourneys.EEU2023_1.3.2.3: Southern Wejherowo & Eastern Kartuzy Counties & the Tricity

EEU2023_PolandPomerania_Ghost.overview: Gdansk Pomerania has supported an economy of agriculture, fishing, and trade for centuries. Its history has been shaped by Polish, Kashubian, and German influences. Poles, Kashubians, and some German families maintained strong Roman Catholic roots and traditions under Prussian rule in the 19th century. Nevertheless, economic and social pressures triggered a wave of emigration to the United States in the four decades leading up to World War I. Immigrants established substantial communities in Chicago, Detroit, Milwaukee, and surrounding rural areas, maintaining strong ethnic and cultural identities as they established themselves in a new land.

SEUR2019_1.5.1.name: Slovenia & Northwest Croatia
SEUR2019_1.5.1.overview: While the western and eastern edges of modern-day Slovenia were historically and culturally aligned with Italy and Hungary, central Slovenia was aligned with Austria and Croatia. Slovenia was one of the longest-held Habsburg provinces, but it was also one of the most rural and agricultural. Cities were sparsely populated, and most people relied on the land. Numerous foreign influences enriched Slovenian urban culture, while the shared peasant experience gave locals a deep appreciation for their country’s natural beauty and folk traditions.

IRL2018_1.2.6.name: Leinster

subjourneys.IRL2021_L_2.1.1: South Kildare, North Carlow & West Wicklow

IRL2018_1.2.6.overview: The varied landscape of south Leinster—from the Wicklow Mountains to the fertile farmland of Carlow and Kilkenny—has impacted the lives of those who lived there. Long-standing ties to Newfoundland fisheries led some to travel to North America in the 18th and early 19th centuries. South Leinster saw less death and misery during the Great Famine than other parts of Ireland because of the region’s productive farmland, but some residents still immigrated to England, Australia, or American states along the Eastern Seaboard such as New York and Pennsylvania.

SEUR2019_2.1.name: Southeastern Sicily
SEUR2019_2.1.overview: Commanding a strategic position in the Mediterranean Sea, Sicily has been a crossroads of civilizations since antiquity. As a result, the Sicilian language includes elements from Latin, Greek, Spanish, Arabic, Norman, German, and other languages. Eastern Sicily is separated from southern Italy by the Strait of Messina. Not far from the strait is Mount Etna, the tallest active volcano in Europe. Taking advantage of volcanic soils, eastern Sicilians farmed some of the most fertile land on the island. Important crops included wheat and citrus fruit. Sulfur became a key export in the Industrial Revolution.

EEU2023_Russia_Ghost.name: Russia

subjourneys.EEU2023_4.2.5: Western Russia & Southern Omsk, Novosibirsk & Amur Oblasts

EEU2023_Russia_Ghost.overview: Russians live in a vast land, stretching from Eastern Europe to the Pacific Ocean. The Russian Empire was the third largest in history, and modern-day Russia is the largest and one of the most populous countries in the world. Ethnic Russians belonging to the Russian Orthodox faith usually made up most of the population, but Russia’s ethnic, linguistic, and religious diversity have contributed to its historical and cultural development. In turn, Russian contributions to the arts, science, sport, architecture, philosophy, and literature have had a major impact beyond its borders.

SCAND2018_1.4.name: Central Sweden
SCAND2018_1.4.overview: Swedes in the 18th century dealt with famine and war. In the century that followed, industrialization and reforms such as mass education altered life fundamentally. As better medicine and foods were developed, the population grew. Eventually, the scarcity of land and the desire for greater opportunity led many to seek the vast frontier of America where Swedes from the Värmland and Dalarna regions made up some of the largest migrant populations. Swedish-Americans took up a prominent place in American society in the Upper Middle West as farmers, politicians, and urban workers.

SCAND2018_5.3.5.name: Denmark
SCAND2018_5.3.5.overview: Most Danes in the 18th and 19th centuries lived as poor farmers in small villages, growing grains and beans, rearing cattle, and sometimes fishing. A small class of artisans and traders worked in the cities and villages. Danish farmers had few rights and were required by law to stay in their village and work for the local landowners. Beginning in the mid-19th century, many Danish farmers and laborers sought religious freedom, land, and higher wages in America. They went to Utah, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Illinois, Iowa, and Nebraska, and they integrated quickly into American life.

SCAND2018_6.1.name: Western Finland

subjourneys.SCAND2018_6.1.2: West Coast of Finland & the Åland Islands
subjourneys.SCAND2018_6.1.1: Southern Ostrobothnia, Northern Satakunta & Northern Pirkanmaa

SCAND2018_6.1.overview: Finns along the country’s southwest coast in the 18th century made a living seal hunting, fishing, and farming. Most peasants owned their own land, but the climate was harsh, with periodic droughts as well as cold. For those who didn’t speak Swedish—the language of the ruling class—participating in civic life could be difficult. In the late 19th century, rapid population growth, poor harvests, and widespread famine spurred many Finns to emigrate and establish large Finnish communities in America.

DE_2021_1.3.1_1.3.3_Ghost.name: Northwestern Germany

subjourneys.DE_2021_1.3.1.2.1: Gütersloh to Bad Oeynhausen to Dissen am Teutoburger Wald
subjourneys.DE_2021_1.3.1.2.3: Eastern North Rhine-Westphalia & Southeastern Lower Saxony
subjourneys.DE_2021_1.3.3.1.3: Rheine, Germany to Emmen, the Netherlands
subjourneys.DE_2021_1.3.1.2.2.2: Bad Essen to Lübbecke to Spenge
subjourneys.DE_2021_1.3.1.3.2.2: Aurich to Papenburg, Germany to Winschoten, the Netherlands
subjourneys.DE_2021_1.3.1.2.1.1: Gütersloh to Bielefeld to Dissen am Teutoburger Wald

DE_2021_1.3.1_1.3.3_Ghost.overview: Northwest Germany’s landscape includes coastal marshlands and rolling farmland. The cities of Emden, Bremen, and Hamburg long dominated Germany’s trade with Europe, while further inland, cattle and flax provided people in the mostly rural region with a stable livelihood. Slower to industrialize, this region saw rapid population growth, prompting many to emigrate to the United States in the 19th century. These German immigrants settled in the rural Midwest in cities like St. Louis and Cincinnati, bringing their brewing culture and strong Lutheran faith along with them.

France2021_1.1.5.2.name: France
France2021_1.1.5.2.overview: Early modern France was shaped by agriculture. Farmers far outnumbered any other profession, but the work was grueling and subject to temperamental weather and exploitative landlords. With the end of the 18th century, the working classes grew increasingly dissatisfied with their economic position, leading to the French Revolution and France’s first constitution. In the two centuries that followed, French citizenry withstood five republics, two empires, and four years of occupation by Nazi Germany. Throughout this time, Paris attracted people from every region of France, which transformed it into the beacon of art, culture, and cuisine it is today.

GreatBritain_2021_2.3.1_2.3.2_2.3.3_Ghos.name: Scottish Highlands & the Hebrides

subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_2.3.2.3: Southern Inner Hebrides & Southwestern Highlands Coast

GreatBritain_2021_2.3.1_2.3.2_2.3.3_Ghos.overview: Highlanders had lived for centuries among the rugged mountains and deep lochs of northern Scotland. They spoke Gaelic and lived in clans bound together by loyalty to their ancestry and their land. The Highlands were transformed in the 1700s and 1800s by the destruction of the traditional clan system and the ensuing Highland Clearances. Dispossessed of their land, many Highlanders sought new lives in the industrial cities of the Lowlands, North America, and New Zealand.

EJ2019_2.2.name: Ashkenazi Jews in Central & Eastern Europe
EJ2019_2.2.overview: Jewish communities in Europe have faced the same difficulty as countless minority groups through history: forcibly separated from mainstream society, then treated with suspicion, disdain, or even punishment for being separate. Until the late 19th century, poverty and discrimination were daily realities for many European Jews, culminating in the horrors of the Holocaust in the 1930s and 1940s. Throughout their history, European Jewish communities have forged strong bonds with one another over shared hardships, channeling their pain into art, literature, philanthropy, intellectual pursuits, and a particularly Jewish brand of humor.

LA2023_SpainSouthEast_Ghost.name: Southern Spain
LA2023_SpainSouthEast_Ghost.overview: In Spain’s southern provinces, people relied on ports and agriculture in a climate ideal for olives and wine. When other regions industrialized, the south lagged behind, suffering from political conflict and a divided class system. This long history of hardship, however, also forged a resilient and vibrant culture, famously expressed through the passionate art of flamenco. In the 20th century, many left for the United States, while those at home endured decades of dictatorship under Francisco Franco.

GreatBritain_2021_2.4.3.name: Northeast Scotland & Orkney & the Shetland Islands
GreatBritain_2021_2.4.3.overview: The history, culture, and DNA of the Far North and Northern Isles of Scotland are heavily influenced by its Scandinavian heritage. Originally part of the Kingdom of Norway, Caithness was recognized as fully Scottish in the 13th century. However, Orkney and Shetland remained Norwegian possessions for an additional 200 years. Even after becoming part of Scotland, the region retained its distinctive culture, language, and legal system. Surrounded by the sea, the hardy and hard-working inhabitants frequently sought their fortunes elsewhere, traveling the world as seafarers, soldiers, traders, and explorers.

GreatBritain_2021_2.3.4.name: Southern Hebrides & Southwestern Scottish Highlands
GreatBritain_2021_2.3.4.overview: The rugged landscape of the Western Highlands and Islands of Scotland has shaped the lives of the people who lived there for centuries. Bound by ties of clan and family, Highlanders were self sufficient and eked out a simple living from the land. The 1700s and 1800s brought dramatic change as society was transformed and the traditional way of life disintegrated. Dispossessed of their lands through the Highland Clearances, many sought new lives overseas in Canada and elsewhere.

DE_2021_EastGermany_Ghost.name: Central & Eastern Germany

subjourneys.DE_2021_1.1.2.1.5: Karlovy Vary, Czech Republic & German Border Region
subjourneys.DE_2021_1.1.2.1.3: Central Germany & Poland Northern Czech Boarder Region

DE_2021_EastGermany_Ghost.overview: Over the centuries, much of present-day Germany was often ravaged by war, but during the last three hundred years, small village enclaves gave way to modern urban life. As a result of turmoil in Europe in the mid-19th century and because they wanted a better life, many people emigrated to North America, settling in the Midwest. They typically remained in tight-knit communities similar to those they had been accustomed to in Europe.

IRL2018_1.1.1.name: Donegal, Ireland
IRL2018_1.1.1.overview: The rugged Blue Stack Mountains and Swilly and Finn Rivers form the backdrop of County Donegal. A land of rural farms and fishing villages, this region was also shaped by the Scottish Plantations that brought English and Scottish settlers to the area. Poverty, famine, and political and religious conflict led many to migrate. Some left for Scotland or Australia, but the most common destination was the United States, where immigrants created a distinctly Irish-American identity that has become part and parcel of American life.

EEU2023_4.2.1.1.name: Eastern Ukraine
EEU2023_4.2.1.1.overview: Eastern Ukraine, often called the breadbasket of Europe, boasts gentle hills, rich black soil, and a mild continental climate perfect for producing wheat, rye, sunflowers, beets, and other crops. This region’s diverse ethnic groups include Ukrainians, Russians, Jews, Poles, Tartars, and Germans. Eastern Ukrainians are traditionally Christian, and most belong to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine. From the 17th century onwards, eastern Ukraine gradually came under the control of the expanding Russian Empire, with many adopting the Russian language. In the 19th and 20th centuries, as industrialization and revolutions transformed life in Ukraine, millions from the region sought opportunity and safety in North America and Central Asia.

GreatBritain_2021_1.1.2.1_1.1.2.2_1.1.2..name: Greater London to Southern East Midlands

subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_1.1.2.3.1: Northeastern Buckinghamshire, Western Hertfordshire & Southern Bedfordshire
subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_1.1.2.2: Southern East Midlands & Northwestern East of England

GreatBritain_2021_1.1.2.1_1.1.2.2_1.1.2..overview: London is where the Industrial Revolution began, one of the most momentous transformations in human history. Across just a few generations, London and its surrounding counties emerged from cycles of famine and epidemics to become a center of empire. Although the region enjoyed the benefits of Britain’s ascendancy, it also suffered devastation during the World Wars of the 20th century. Londoners rebuilt their lives from the ashes, following the pattern of the generations that preceded them.

SEUR2019_2.2.name: Apulia Region
SEUR2019_2.2.overview: The capital of the Apulia (Puglia) region of southern Italy, Bari has a diverse history of foreign influence. Greeks, Romans, Arabic-speaking Muslims, Norman French, Spaniards, and Austrians have all left traces on its language, culture, cuisine, and people. The medieval German Emperor Frederick II loved this part of his realm so much for its beauty and temperate climate that he said that had God known Puglia, he would not have given the Israelites Palestine for their promised land.

DE_2021_3.4.1.1_1.1.1.3.4_Ghost.name: Switzerland

subjourneys.DE_2021_1.1.1.3.4: Southeast Germany, Western Austria & Eastern Switzerland

DE_2021_3.4.1.1_1.1.1.3.4_Ghost.overview: Nestled in the Alps, Switzerland’s population has been shaped by its rugged terrain as well as by the countries that border it, particularly Germany, France, and Italy. Over the centuries, Switzerland struggled to create a single nation, separated not only by geographic barriers but also by language, religion, and values. With the establishment of its first constitution in 1848, a modern, unified Switzerland was born. Despite its famed principle of neutrality, Switzerland was shaken by both World Wars, but its resilience made it an innovative country whose residents enjoy a high standard of living.

GreatBritain_2021_2.1.2_2.1.3_Ghost.name: Northern Ireland & Southwest Scotland
GreatBritain_2021_2.1.2_2.1.3_Ghost.overview: Just twelve miles apart at their nearest point, northeast Ireland and southwest Scotland have close cultural and historical ties. The first Scottish Protestants moved to the province of Ulster in the 17th century. Since then, the Ulster Scots have experienced ongoing political conflict with the native Irish Catholics. Over the centuries, millions of emigrants from both groups have left Ireland, often seeking an escape from famine or hardship. Large numbers of Ulster Scots ended up in southwest Scotland, England, Australia, and North America.

EEU2023_CzechBohemia_Ghost.overview: Bohemia is the western side of today’s Czechia. Central Bohemia is rich and fertile, while its northern and western edges are rocky and mountainous. German speakers dominated many of these areas until the end of the 19th century, when Czech speakers started running major industries and began a Czech national revival in politics and culture. Still, the region’s cuisine, fashion, and fine arts retained many German influences. Although modern history has been dominated by warfare and industrialization, Bohemian artists managed to leave a mark on Europe before, during, and after the communist era.

EEU2023_UkraineWest_Ghost.overview: The western region of present-day Ukraine is mostly wooded, mountainous, and marked by centuries of rule by central European states such as Poland and the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Its population—referred to in the 19th century as ‘Ruthenians,’ ‘Galicians,’ or ‘Rusyns’—was more likely to speak Ukrainian and belong to the Greek Catholic Orthodox religion than elsewhere in Ukraine. The inhabitants were traditionally poorer, had less land, worse infrastructure, and lower literacy rates than peasants elsewhere in Europe. Beginning in the latter 19th century, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians and Jews from the region immigrated to Western Pennsylvania as well as the plains of Canada and the U.S.

DE_2021_1.1.1_Ghost.name: Baden-Württemberg & Hesse

subjourneys.DE_2021_1.1.1.3.3.1: Lörrach to Bad Krozingen to Waldshut-Tiengen

DE_2021_1.1.1_Ghost.overview: Located at the confluence of the Rhine, Saar, and Mosel rivers, southwest Germany boasts fertile soil, dramatic forests, and captivating mountains. As a borderland between Germany and France, the region witnessed frequent warfare, famine, and government instability, alongside striking linguistic and religious diversity. Farmers, weavers, fruit growers, miners, and brewers all claimed Baden-Württemberg and Hesse as their homeland. However, heavy taxation, population growth, and various weather disasters spurred many residents to look for new opportunities in the most eastern parts of Europe and the United States.

GreatBritain_2021_3.2.5.name: Isle of Man
GreatBritain_2021_3.2.5.overview: Tucked into the Irish Sea between Ireland and Great Britain, the Isle of Man isn’t part of the United Kingdom but is a Crown Dependency, governing itself but following the foreign policy of Britain. The island’s flag bears the triskelion, an image of three armored legs with a spur at each heel. The emblem’s motto, “Wherever you throw it, it will stand,” is fitting for a people that have weathered many changes, both in their island home and in the new homes they made in foreign lands.

GreatBritain_2021_1.3.2.name: Birmingham

subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_1.3.2.2.2: Dudley, Sandwell, Southwestern Birmingham & Northeastern Worcestershire

GreatBritain_2021_1.3.2.overview: By the 1700s, residents of the West Midlands were farmers, miners, or they participated in one of the local industries. Those in Birmingham often labored in workshops creating products for export across England and abroad. During the 19th century, some chose to move to London or the United States in search of factory work or other economic possibilities. Others stayed to enjoy the advancements created by the “civil gospel.” Over the years, the region’s inhabitants and industries adapted many times to suit the needs of war and increasing modernization.

SCAND2018_1.3.name: Southern Sweden
SCAND2018_1.3.overview: Sweden’s southeastern provinces of Skåne and Götaland included rich farmland where families grew barley and raised livestock. Even in Småland, where forests and bogs covered much of the sandy land, the population grew in the early 1800s as settlers cleared and reclaimed swamps and forests. As small villages were broken up in favor of large, individual farmsteads, less available land and a growing population led thousands to leave for America in the late 19th century, where they farmed the vast plains of the Upper Midwest.

EEU2023_PolandSilesia_Ghost.name: South Central Poland

subjourneys.EEU2023_1.1.1.3.1.2: Western Lower Silesian Voivodeship & East-Central Germany
subjourneys.EEU2023_1.1.1.3.4.3: Ostrów Wielkopolski | Grabów nad Prosną | Międzybórz

EEU2023_PolandSilesia_Ghost.overview: South central Poland straddles two historical regions: Lesser Poland, with its capital at Kraków, and Silesia, particularly Upper Silesia. Centered around the north-flowing Odra and Vistula Rivers and their tributaries, the region is a mix of hills and plains, flanked on the south by mountains from the Sudeten and Carpathian ranges. This geography has fostered both agricultural and industrial activity, especially coal and mineral mining. Over the centuries, the region has seen devastating wars, shifts in territorial control, and economic and cultural transformations that have profoundly shaped the lives of its inhabitants, including Poles, Germans, Czechs, Jews, and others. At times, these changes spurred migration, both regionally and across the Atlantic.

MENA2019_1.4.2.2.2_1.4.2.2.3.name: Romania
MENA2019_1.4.2.2.2_1.4.2.2.3.overview: The people of Romania have a complicated, eventful, and rich history. Each province has its own unique trajectory, as empires going back all the way to the Romans traded control of territories. This resulted in great ethnic, cultural, and linguistic diversity. Some of the ethnicities modern Romanians belong or can trace their roots back to are Hungarian-speaking Székelys, Saxon Germans, Jews, Roma, and Greeks, to name a few, and this mix of cultures is reflected in the foods, architecture, and music of Romania.

GreatBritain_2021_1.4.2_1.4.3_Ghost.name: Cornwall

subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_1.4.2.1.3: Camborne to Helston to Carrick Roads

GreatBritain_2021_1.4.2_1.4.3_Ghost.overview: Before industrialization, residents of Cornwall were typically small-scale farmers or fishers. They also had a long history of hard-rock mining, which served them well when global demand for copper and tin increased in the 19th century. Emigrants found that their mining skills were welcomed the world over as they established “Cornishtowns” from Canada to South Africa to New Zealand. Their Celtic roots also persisted in traditional Cornish food and music, which became points of pride both at home and abroad.

DE_2021_1.1.2_Ghost.name: Franconia

subjourneys.DE_2021_1.1.2.1.2: Upper Franconia, Middle Franconia & Upper Palatinate

DE_2021_1.1.2_Ghost.overview: The unique political history of southern Germany helped Franconians develop a separate identity from their Bavarian neighbors. This included their own dialect and Protestant strongholds. Peasant farmers labored under a feudal system until industrialization created new opportunities for them in urban centers. In the 19th century, war and economic hardship caused successive waves of people to leave. Most immigrants settled in German American farming communities across the Upper Midwest. Later immigrants found homes in U.S. industrial centers. Over multiple generations, German immigrants melded into mainstream American society, though they retained much of their heritage and traditions.

GreatBritain_2021_2.1.1.name: Scotland Central Belt

subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_2.1.1.3.4: Falkirk, North Lanarkshire, West Lothian & Surrounding Area
subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_2.1.1.3.2: Falkirk, Clackmannanshire, Southwestern Fife & Surrounding Area

GreatBritain_2021_2.1.1.overview: The 1700s and 1800s saw central Scotland transformed from a mostly rural landscape into the “Workshop of the World,” with Lowland Scots increasingly concentrated in mining villages, industrial towns, and growing cities. The Scottish Enlightenment brought the ideas of Scotland’s thinkers to the world, and the population swelled as new industries attracted workers. However, many industries were subject to economic downturns and these, along with poor living conditions, led some Scots to seek new lives overseas in North America and throughout the British Empire into the 20th century.

DE_2021_1.3.2.1.3.name: Belgium
DE_2021_1.3.2.1.3.overview: Belgium, culturally divided between the Dutch-speaking Flemish in the north and the French-speaking Walloons in the south, has long been known for its medieval universities, Renaissance tapestries, and castle-dotted villages. Beginning in the modern period, it transformed from a largely rural collection of towns to an economic and political center of Europe. Having set the stage for some of the most decisive moments in the Napoleonic Wars and both world wars, this growth was not without its hardships, but Belgians persevered, thanks in part to their high degree of political and social involvement.

EEU2023_PolandMasovia_Ghost.name: Mazovia

subjourneys.EEU2023_3.1.3.1.4: Western Przasnysz, Northern Maków & West Central Ostrołęka Counties
subjourneys.EEU2023_3.1.1.1.2: Northern Lublin & Central & Southern Mazovian Voivodeships

EEU2023_PolandMasovia_Ghost.overview: The fertile lands of the Mazovia region, centered around the capital city of Warsaw in east-central Poland, have been used to grow grains and raise animals for centuries. With deep roots in Roman Catholicism, ethnic Poles have built pilgrimage sites and ornate churches across the region’s rolling hills. The balm of faith offered comfort amid the political and economic upheaval of the 18th and 19th centuries. Starting in the late 1800s, Mazovian immigrants contributed significantly to Poland's now-extensive diaspora. Some 20 million people of Polish heritage live outside of Poland today, with large populations in Chicago and the cities of the U.S. Northeast.

DE_2021_7.1.name: Catholic Black Sea Germans

subjourneys.DE_2021_7.1.1: Black Sea Germans in Bessarabia, Kutschurgan, Beresan & Liebental
subjourneys.DE_2021_7.1.1.1: Black Sea Germans—Strassburg, Elsass, Kandel, Selz

DE_2021_7.1.overview: Catholic Germans living in the Holy Roman Empire endured generations of wars, high taxes, scarcity of land, and religious intolerance after the Reformation. Napoleon brought more unrest to the region, driving some Germans from their homes in the southern German states and Alsace. So, when the chance came to move to the Russian Empire where there was plenty of land and promises of freedom, thousands of families settled in provinces along the Black Sea. Life changed again as their freedoms were revoked. Some stayed in Russia and faced more unrest and war, but many moved again to start a new life in North America.

GreatBritain_2021_3.1.1_3.1.2_3.1.3_Ghos.name: East Midlands, Yorkshire & North England

subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_3.1.2.2: West Yorkshire, Eastern Greater Manchester & Surrounding Area
subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_3.1.2.2.2: East of Manchester to West of Wakefield

GreatBritain_2021_3.1.1_3.1.2_3.1.3_Ghos.overview: In the early 1700s, residents of Yorkshire lived on farms and in market towns. The Industrial Revolution began a series of staggering changes. For some, changes meant new economic opportunities. For many others, it meant long workdays, perilous jobs, and overcrowded living quarters. This new pace of life drove migration, not only south to London but also abroad, to the United States, Canada, and Australia. Two world wars further transformed Yorkshire’s traditional culture and loosened its social bonds. A new youth-based counterculture emerged to remake the postwar world.

LA2023_Madeira_Ghost.name: Madeira

subjourneys.LA2023_1.4.1.1: Guyana, Grenada & St Vincent & the Grenadines

LA2023_Madeira_Ghost.overview: Named for its lush, forested terrain (madeira means “wood” in Portuguese), the archipelago of Madeira lies 700 miles southwest of mainland Portugal. From the 1400s, islanders cultivated grains, sugarcane, and grapes on terraced mountainsides, developing a thriving wine industry that would gain international renown. Madeira wine became a key export, even gracing tables during the American Revolution, but overcrowding, poverty, and political upheaval prompted waves of emigration, and by the turn of the 20th century, thousands of Madeirans had arrived in Hawaii to work on sugar plantations. They brought with them their rich cultural traditions, including cuisine and music.

EEU2023_LesserPoland_Ghost.overview: Southeast Poland encompasses part of a region historically known as Lesser Poland or Western Galicia. Its landscape features dense forests, meandering rivers, and open meadows stretching from the rolling Carpathian foothills to the fertile plains of the Vistula River valley. The area has featured remarkable ethnic diversity, including Poles, Ukrainians, Jews, and others, who generally coexisted peacefully. While most inhabitants farmed the land, others lived in market towns and cities such as Kraków that were built around medieval squares. During the 19th and 20th centuries, widespread poverty drove significant migration to North America.

EEU2023_GreaterPoland_Ghost.name: West Central Poland

subjourneys.EEU2023_1.3.1.3: East Central Greater Poland & West Central Kuyavian–Pomeranian Voivodeships
subjourneys.EEU2023_1.1.1.3.2.1: Central & Southern Lubusz Voivodeship & German Border

EEU2023_GreaterPoland_Ghost.overview: Greater Poland, a region in west-central Poland, has been called the “cradle of Poland” due to its critical role in the formation of the Polish state in the 10th century. Witness to repeated wars and shifting control over the centuries, it emerged as a center of Polish resistance and uprising. Inhabited by Poles and other ethnic groups—Jews, Lithuanians, Russians, and Germans, among others—and anchored by ancient cities such as Poznan and Toruń, this low-lying region has been known for its diverse agricultural output. But political, cultural, and economic pressures led many to immigrate to the United States in the 19th and 20th centuries.

GreatBritain_2021_3.2.2.2_1.3.3_Ghost.name: Wales

subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_1.3.3: Central & Southern Wales & England Border Counties
subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_1.3.3.1: Mid Wales, South East Wales & Surrounding Area

GreatBritain_2021_3.2.2.2_1.3.3_Ghost.overview: Living in a land known for its landscape, castles, and distinctive Celtic language, the Welsh were largely a rural, farming folk before the Industrial Revolution. Coal mining and metalsmithing quickly transformed the country, and the overcrowding, disease, and wage disputes that followed drove some Welsh communities to immigrate to the United States in the 19th century. Those who stayed felt the effects of the Great Depression just as Welsh Americans did, and many abandoned the mines to find work in larger cities, including Cardiff and London.

SEUR2019_2.4.name: North Italy
SEUR2019_2.4.overview: Since the 18th century, northern Italy has included various political states, languages, and cultures. In Lombardy, Piedmont, and Tuscany, people farmed the rich plains and built a world-renowned textile industry. Seamen and merchants of the Ligurian coast excelled in international trade. Tuscans were well known for manufacturing. These regional specialties made northern Italy an important agricultural and industrial center. In addition to economic forces, Roman Catholicism has also shaped the lives of the people of this region.

EEU2023_Estonia_Ghost.name: Estonia
EEU2023_Estonia_Ghost.overview: Estonia features dense forests and marshland, with a mild northern climate producing long summer days and cold winter nights. Its small size and location made it vulnerable to powerful neighbors, but also made it an important center of exchange between German lands, Scandinavia, and Russia. Ethnic Estonians are closely related to Finns in language and customs, but for centuries they were under the control of German noblemen and Russian imperial rule. In the 20th century, amidst a series of destructive wars, revolutions, and occupations, many Estonians settled in new locations, such as the United States, Australia, and Canada. But throughout their history, Estonians have maintained a vibrant culture and a strong sense of nationhood.

SCAND2018_6.3.name: Ostrobothnia, Central Ostrobothnia & South Ostrobothnia, Finland
SCAND2018_6.3.overview: In the provinces of Vaasa and southern Bothnia, ethnic Finns and Swedes lived side by side for centuries, harvesting seals and fish, timber, and grain. This region had some of the largest populations of Swedish speakers in all of Finland, and Swedish influence on laws, language, and culture was strong into the 20th century. Throughout the 18th and 19th century, its coastal communities were vulnerable to raids by the British and Russians, but they also benefited from trading timber, tar, paper, and dairy products with the world.

SCAND2018_3.3.name: Southern & Southwestern Norway
SCAND2018_3.3.overview: Marked by fjords, harbor towns, and sparsely populated inland valleys, life along the southern coast of Norway offered economic opportunities for many. Small farmers could supplement their diet and income with fishing. Others logged, built ships, and fished, but this work could become a casualty of global events. Although shipbuilding and timber boomed in the mid-19th century, when shipyards failed to transition to steam in the 1880s, thousands of southern Norwegian workers and their families left for America where land and work were available.

SCAND2018_3.2.name: Eastern Norway
SCAND2018_3.2.overview: In the 1700s Norway’s population was mostly rural. Most farmers owned or leased their land, a small class of merchants and bureaucrats lived in the cities, and Norway’s rich natural resources led to rising wealth through trade. However, a steep increase in population in the 19th century combined with a scarcity of land, led many of Eastern Norway’s farmers and city-dwellers to look for greater prosperity in America. Once there, Norwegians made up one of the most tight-knit immigrant communities in the Upper Midwest.

DE_2021_Netherlands_Ghost.name: The Netherlands

subjourneys.DE_2021_1.3.2.2.3.2: Beilan, Netherlands to Bad Bentheim, Germany

DE_2021_Netherlands_Ghost.overview: Until the end of the 18th century, the Netherlands was renowned for its prowess in international trade. A third of the Dutch population lived in cities, working in trade or processing raw materials. Rural Dutch fished, raised livestock, and cultivated grain. But fishing and trade declined by the 19th century. Poverty and religious disputes prompted large-scale immigration. The American Midwest was the most common destination for Dutch immigrants before World War II. After the war, immigration targeted a wider range of destinations.

GreatBritain_2021_1.2.1_1.3.1_Ghost.name: Central Southern England

subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_1.2.1.3: Central South East England & Greater London
subjourneys.GreatBritain_2021_1.3.1: Northeastern South West England & Northwestern South East England

GreatBritain_2021_1.2.1_1.3.1_Ghost.overview: For centuries, residents of central southern England lived in a landscape dotted with market towns and farming villages, part of a traditional Royalist and Church of England stronghold. The effects of the Industrial Revolution and agricultural revolution came on gradually, but over time they pushed thousands of people out of the countryside and into London or faraway Australia or America. During both world wars, southern England suffered direct attacks, but the region showed resilience in determinedly remaking itself.

SCAND2018_3.1.name: Western Norway
SCAND2018_3.1.overview: Norway’s western coast winds for hundreds of miles, punctuated by fjords, fishing villages, and farms. For centuries, Norwegians there fished for cod and herring. Although life was often tenuous, the farmers and fishers in western Norway were well fed and prosperous compared to other places in Europe. Fish was the main export, but residents also relied on subsistence farming and timber. As the population grew in the 19th century, migrants from the Sognefjord and Hardangerfjord regions left for America to live in Wisconsin, Minnesota, and North Dakota.

ASIA2023_3.3.2.4.name: Fiji
ASIA2023_3.3.2.4.overview: Early settlers first voyaged to the Fiji archipelago 3,500 years ago and formed an indigenous Fijian language and culture. The presence of Lapita pottery suggests origins in the Melanesian region, and Fijian oral traditions recount ongoing voyaging to and exchange with neighboring Tonga and Sāmoa. Complex local chiefdoms warred across scores of inhabited islands, spanning 600 miles from west to east. Inland communities on Lau Island cultivated yams and taro and built defensive ditches and moats. The Lasakau, Soso, and other people of the sea maintained coastal communities and fished along rivers and on the open ocean.

ASIA2023_3.3.1.1.2.name: Polynesia
ASIA2023_3.3.1.1.2.overview: For thousands of years, Polynesian ancestors viewed the Pacific Ocean as a sea of islands traversable by outrigger and double-hulled canoes. Voyagers from western Oceania traveled to Fiji, Tonga, Sāmoa, and on to the Marquesas; from there, they settled Tahiti, Hawai‘i, Rapa Nui, the Cook Islands, Aotearoa-New Zealand, and other islands. The region had no sustained contact with the outside world until British and French explorers arrived in the 1700s. By the early 1900s, steamships and aircraft had dramatically increased trade and migration. World War II, outmigration, and modern tourism further integrated the region with the world beyond Oceania.

ASIA2023_3.3.2.3.name: Tonga
ASIA2023_3.3.2.3.overview: Early settlers first migrated to the Tongan archipelago 3,200 years ago as part of the Lapita expansion that also settled neighboring Fiji and Sāmoa. According to Tongan oral traditions, the demi-god Maui pulled up the islands from the ocean with his magic fishhook. Those traditions also say that the god Tangaloa and a mortal woman were the parents of ‘Aho‘eitu, Tonga’s first divine king. The resulting Tu‘i Tonga Empire forged a trade and cultural network extending to Sāmoa, Fiji, Rotuma, and Vanuatu. The first Tongans and their descendants were skilled builders of long-range canoes, monuments, and langi (terraced tombs).

AUNZ2019_2.1_2.3_2.4_2.5_2.6_2.7_2.10.overview: Great Britain was getting crowded. Convicts couldn’t be sent to the American colonies after they declared independence, prisons were full, and agriculture was near capacity. Australia offered a solution. After the First Fleet arrived in 1788, British colonists grew New South Wales from a rough collection of tents into a network of prosperous cities. The newcomers lived through boom and bust, gold rush and drought. Still, the migrants came, turning a former British colony into a land with a future and culture all its own.

ASIA2023_Hawaii_Ghost.name: Hawaiian Islands
ASIA2023_Hawaii_Ghost.overview: Kanaka Maoli (Native Hawaiian) ancestors first settled Hawai‘i by way of large double-hulled voyaging canoes from the Marquesas and other islands in Polynesia. Mo‘olelo (oral traditions) suggest an initial migration between 1,200 and 2,000 years ago. Approximately 900 years ago, Pāʻao, a high priest from Tahiti, introduced a highly structured social order with ali‘i (chiefs) as the ruling nobility. To sustain their communities, early Hawaiians built lo‘i (irrigated terraces) to grow kalo (taro), which became Hawai‘i’s staple crop. They also constructed loko i‘a (fishponds) for a steady supply of ‘ama‘ama (mullet) and other marine resources.

LA2023_1.4.3.name: Portuguese in Hawaii & California
LA2023_1.4.3.overview: Known for their agricultural skills, residents of Portugal’s Azores and Madeira islands were often pushed by poverty and instability to seek new lives in the United States. In their primary destinations of Hawaii and California, they found work on plantations, on farms, and as business owners. In both places, they built strong communities, preserving unique traditions like the Holy Ghost Festival while also contributing to local culture, famously adapting their braguinha into the beloved ukulele.

SEUR2019_2.7.name: Calabria
SEUR2019_2.7.overview: Forming the toe of Italy’s boot-shaped peninsula, Calabria lies in the heart of southern Italy. The name “Italy” comes from this region, as the ancient residents of Calabria were known as Italoi in Greek. Known for their silk production and warm climate, Calabrians were nonetheless plagued by natural disasters and poverty in the 19th and early 20th centuries. Many uprooted their lives in search of better living conditions. Often they chose the United States, where millions of Italian immigrants embraced American culture and left an indelible mark on its entertainment, language, and cuisine.

AUNZ2019_1.6.name: Western Australia, European & British Settlers
AUNZ2019_1.6.overview: Western Australia’s first British immigrants were free settlers, but the colony soon took in convicts as laborers. The colony was remote, connected to other Australian settlements by sea, but the discovery of gold brought fortune seekers from across the continent. Western Australia’s farmers helped meet the demands of two world wars, which brought other changes as well. During World War I, a rail route finally made the state more accessible to tourists and traders. Later came submarine bases, code-breaking units, fortifications, and changes in women’s roles.

AUNZ2019_1.2.name: Victoria, Australia, European & British Settlers

subjourneys.AUNZ2019_1.2.1: Great South Coast, Victoria, European & British Settlers

AUNZ2019_1.2.overview: As wealthy sheep farmers sought more land, Melbourne (and later Victoria) was established as a direct offshoot of Van Diemen’s Land. In the middle of the 19th century the population was shaped by gold rushes, as migrants arrived to seek their fortune. Melbourne developed into a culturally diverse city and was home to the first Australian Parliament after Federation. Industries grew on the city’s outskirts during the early 20th century, and Melbourne developed an expressive, creative sense of fun that continues today.

ASIA2023_Samoa_Ghost.name: Samoan Islands
ASIA2023_Samoa_Ghost.overview: Sāmoa is located between Hawai‘i and New Zealand (or Aotearoa, the Māori-language name) in Oceania’s Polynesian region. Early settlers voyaged to the islands 3,500 years ago as part of the Lapita expansion that also settled Fiji and Tonga. The Samoan people have a rich oral tradition and are guided by fa‘aSāmoa (the Samoan way of life, culture, and values), which emphasizes ‘aiga (extended family), communal living, mutual respect, and the fa‘amatai (chiefly leadership system). Once a center of European rivalry, Sāmoa was divided in 1899 between Germany and the United States. Western Sāmoa (now Sāmoa) gained independence in 1962; American Sāmoa remains a U.S. territory.

ASIA2023_5.name: Guam
ASIA2023_5.overview: Guam (Guåhan in the Indigenous Chamorro language) is the largest and southernmost island of the Mariana Archipelago in the northwestern Pacific Islands region. The Chamorro people have called the archipelago home for 3,500 years. An extended period of Spanish influence began in the 1500s. Later, the United States took control of Guam in 1898 after the Spanish-American War, while Germany and subsequently Japan controlled the Northern Marianas. After World War II, the United States regained Guam and took over the northern islands, which remain U.S. territories. Although a popular slogan celebrates Guam as “Where America’s Day Begins,” the archipelago's Indigenous identity persists.

AUNZ2019_2.2.name: Queensland, European & British Settlers
AUNZ2019_2.2.overview: European settlement in Queensland began with an outpost for convicts, housing the roughest reoffenders. The prison eventually closed, and the area opened to free settlers looking for land. Vast distances between settlements left rural residents dependent on transport and communication systems, even for education and medical services. During the world wars, Queensland was an important hub for training soldiers, while an active home front sent provisions to the front lines. Emigration plans after World War II introduced new multicultural influences to Queensland’s urban centers.

AUNZ2019_1.4.name: South Australia, European & British Settlers
AUNZ2019_1.4.overview: South Australia was planned and populated under a careful emigration plan intended to create the ideal colony. Mineral deposits, including gold and opal, led to thriving mining and refining industries, and the colony became the home of Australian female suffrage. The flat landscape lent itself to bicycles and automobiles, which residents were quick to adopt. The land also proved good for vineyards. During the war years, the colony turned to manufacturing household appliances, automobiles, and (later) military supplies. Wine and manufacturing continue to help define South Australian culture.

AUNZ2019_1.5.name: Tasmania, European & British Settlers
AUNZ2019_1.5.overview: When the British occupied the rugged, mountainous island surrounded by the Southern Ocean and Tasman Sea in 1803, they decided it made an ideal prison. Today more than half of Tasmania’s population descends from the 73,000 convicts sent to the penal colony. Wealthy settlers also came from Britain, enticed by the promise of land. The population boom ended when thousands emigrated to the Victorian gold fields. As the 20th century opened, Tasmania was attracting tourists, while its own often left to mainland cities for work.

ASIA2023_NewZealand_Ghost.name: New Zealand
ASIA2023_NewZealand_Ghost.overview: Aotearoa, the Māori name for New Zealand, is an island nation in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists primarily of two main islands: Te Ika-a-Māui (North Island) and Te Waipounamu (South Island). The subtropical North Island was the landing place of the first Māori inhabitants, who migrated from eastern Polynesia beginning in the 1300s. Although the arrival of European (Pākehā) settlers in the late 1700s profoundly changed Māori life, the culture has remained deeply rooted in whakapapa, the genealogical bonds between generations and the world they inhabit.

AUNZ2019_1.1.overview: The first non-Māori (Pākehā) occupants of New Zealand were mostly whalers and seal hunters. Their increasingly lawless behavior led to Britain making the islands an official British colony in 1840. As more colonists came to establish European-style farming and populate the land, tensions between the indigenous Māori and Pākehā led to fighting. Sheep and dairy farming gained a foothold, supported by a traveling workforce. Women increasingly participated in politics and employment, and by World War II were required to enter the workforce.
